fields.title: The Key Teachings of R. A. Torrey
fields.subtitle: An Ochorus companion to his life and teaching
fields.description: A concise, faithful guide to the heart of R. A. Torrey’s message — the Holy Spirit as a Person to be known, the baptism with the Spirit as power for service, prayer, Bible study, personal soul-winning and the fundamentals of the faith — and the single conviction beneath it all: that God means exactly what He says. Eighteen short chapters, each ending in questions and a prayer, written by Ochorus as a companion to Torrey’s own public-domain works, which readers are warmly encouraged to go to directly.
fields.about_html:
This is not a book by R. A. Torrey. It is a companion to him — an independent work of exposition and appreciation, written by Ochorus, that gathers the heart of his teaching into eighteen short chapters for the ordinary reader, with a chapter on his life, a conclusion and a guide to his books.

Torrey’s one conviction was that God has spoken plainly and means what He says. The doubter who had once taken the Bible apart at Yale spent fifty years taking it at its word: on the Holy Spirit, who is a Person and not an influence; on the power for service that the Father promises to those who ask; on prayer, on the Scriptures, on the deity and atonement of Christ, on assurance, on the winning of souls, and on the solemn realities of judgement and the Lord’s return. This volume follows that thread, weighs honestly where he must be read with care — above all his teaching on the baptism with the Spirit as a distinct experience after conversion, and the blunt certainty of his manner — and ends each chapter as he would have wished, with something to do and a prayer.

Torrey’s own writings are in the public domain and freely available, and every chapter here names them so the reader can go to the source; several of his books and sermons are in the Ochorus library. This companion is offered only to open the door. It quotes Scripture from the Authorised (King James) Version, and it makes no claim to stand in for the man’s own plain, direct and urgent pages.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
God is not a man, that he should lie; neither the son of man, that he should repent: hath he said, and shall he not do it? or hath he spoken, and shall he not make it good? NUMBERS 23:19

Reuben Archer Torrey was one of the best-known Christian teachers in the English-speaking world at the turn of the twentieth century, and one of the least colourful. He had none of D. L. Moody’s warmth of anecdote or Spurgeon’s wit. He was a bearded, precise man from a wealthy family, educated at Yale and in Germany, who was content to be told he was no orator. And yet crowds of many thousands came to hear him on four continents, a generation of Bible-school students learned their trade from him, and his small handbooks on prayer, the Holy Spirit and personal evangelism have never quite gone out of print.

One conviction beneath the others

The reason is not hard to find. Torrey believed, with a completeness that is rare, that God has spoken plainly and means exactly what He says. That was the whole of him.

For ever, O LORD, thy word is settled in heaven. PSALM 119:89

Almost everything Torrey taught follows from this one habit of mind. Is a believer unsure whether he is saved? Show him what God says in John 3:36, and let him believe God rather than his feelings. Has a worker no power in his service? The Father has promised the Holy Spirit to them that ask Him; let him ask, and believe that he has received. Is a Christian weak and defeated? God has provided a risen Saviour and an indwelling Spirit; let him look to them. Is a man careless of his soul? God has spoken of judgement; let him be told, plainly and in love. The phrase that recurs through his books is some form of because God says so. That is the thread through every chapter of this volume.

Why he still matters

Torrey is worth reading for at least two reasons.

The first is that he made the Holy Spirit personal to a great many Christians who had thought of Him as an influence, a vague warmth or a force to be harnessed. His insistence that the Spirit is a Person, who knows, wills, loves and can be grieved, is one of the most useful things any teacher has said to the ordinary believer.

The second is that he was relentlessly practical. His books tell you what to do: how long to read your Bible each day, what to pray for in the morning and what to confess at night, what passage to open when a friend says he is too great a sinner to be saved. There is very little vague spirituality in him. He believed that ordinary Christians could be taught to pray, to study and to lead others to Christ, and he spent his life teaching them.

How this book is arranged

After a chapter on his life, eighteen short chapters set out his teaching. The first five concern the Holy Spirit: His personality, the baptism with the Spirit, how that blessing is sought, how power is renewed and lost, and the Spirit’s work in setting the believer free. Then come prayer, praying in the Spirit, Bible study and the difficulties of the Bible. Four chapters follow on the fundamentals he defended — the deity of Christ, the atonement, justification and the new birth, and assurance. Three concern the Christian’s life and witness: beginning right, bringing others to Christ, and preaching the uplifted Christ. The last two take up the resurrection and the return of the Lord, and the hardest subject of all, everlasting punishment.

Each chapter ends with application points and a prayer. Torrey would have approved. He had little patience for truth that did not issue in action, and he closed nearly every sermon with a direct call to do something now.

Where he must be read with care

This is not a book of hero-worship, and it is better to say plainly at the start where Torrey must be weighed rather than simply received.

First, his best-known teaching, that the baptism with the Holy Spirit is a definite experience distinct from and subsequent to regeneration, is disputed by many careful students of the same Scriptures, who read 1 Corinthians 12:13 as teaching that every believer is baptised by the Spirit at conversion, and who prefer to speak of repeated fillings rather than a second blessing. Torrey’s teaching has blessed many and troubled some. Chapters four to six set it out as he gave it and say where it needs qualification.

For by one Spirit are we all baptized into one body, whether we be Jews or Gentiles, whether we be bond or free; and have been all made to drink into one Spirit. 1 CORINTHIANS 12:13

Second, Torrey’s certainty could become bluntness, and his bluntness could become harshness. He wrote that any Christian worker who had not received the baptism with the Spirit ought to stop work at once; he offered seven steps which, taken, would lead with absolute certainty into the blessing; he spoke of his opponents in terms no gentle reader will enjoy. His confidence was often a gift. It could also crush the tender conscience and flatten real complexity.

Third, he argued in the manner of his time. His apologetics lean heavily on the rational force of evidence, and some of his arguments and illustrations have dated. The truths he defended have not dated, but the reader should not assume that every argument he used for them is the best one.

And fourth, on eternal punishment and the return of Christ he spoke with a directness that may shock a modern reader. This book does not soften what he taught, but it tries to hold it as Scripture does: soberly, and with tears.

Why read him, then? Because on the central matter he was right. God does mean what He says. The counsel of this book is the counsel of Scripture: Prove all things; hold fast that which is good (1 Thessalonians 5:21). Where Torrey is faithful, and he usually is, take God at His word as he did. Where he presses further than the text, set that aside and lose nothing.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Name one promise of God that you believe in principle but do not act upon. Write it down and keep it where you will see it while you read this book.

2. Ask yourself honestly whether you trust your feelings or God’s word more when the two disagree.

3. Choose a pace for this book — a chapter a day or one a week — and decide now when you will read it.

4. Resolve to check every claim in these pages, and every claim of Torrey’s, against the Bible itself.

5. Ask God to use this book not to make you admire a teacher but to make you pray, study and speak for Christ.

A PRAYER
Faithful God, You are not a man that You should lie. What You have said, You will do, and what You have spoken, You will make good.
Forgive me for the promises I have admired and never believed, and the commands I have honoured and never obeyed.
As I read of Your servant Reuben Torrey, teach me to take You at Your word as he did, and keep me from his faults as well as from my own.
Send me not to him but to Christ, and to the Scriptures, and to my knees. Amen.

fields.title: The Doubter Who Was Sent
fields.body_html:
Also I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Then said I, Here am I; send me. ISAIAH 6:8

A privileged boyhood. Reuben Archer Torrey was born on the twenty-eighth of January, 1856, in Hoboken, New Jersey, into a family of comfortable wealth. He wanted for nothing that money could buy. His mother was a woman of earnest faith who prayed for her son for years, and, by his own later account, hoped that he would one day preach the gospel. He had no intention of doing so. He went up to Yale at fifteen, and there he gave himself to the pleasures open to a rich young man — the theatre, cards, horse-racing and a good deal of drink — and to the pleasure of argument. He read the new criticism of the Bible and enjoyed it. He was clever, and he knew it.

A night at Yale. In his final year at Yale, in 1875, that life came to a sudden end. Torrey later told how, sick of himself and of everything, he resolved one night to take his own life. Instead he found himself on his knees. He remembered his mother’s prayers, and he promised God that if He would deliver him he would do whatever He asked, even if it meant preaching. He rose a changed man, and he never went back on the promise. He made a public profession of faith, graduated from Yale College that year, and entered the Yale divinity school, completing his course in 1878.

The doubter answered. Conversion did not end his questions. He had absorbed, and for a time kept, the critical views of Scripture he had admired as a student, and he was ordained to the Congregational ministry in 1878 still wrestling with them. He took a small church at Garrettsville, Ohio, and in 1879 married Clara Smith, who was his partner for the rest of his life. Then, in 1882, he did something characteristic. Rather than settle his doubts at second hand, he went to Germany, to the universities of Leipzig and Erlangen, and sat under some of the leading scholars of the day. He came home holding a higher view of the Bible than the one he had taken with him. From then on he defended the Scriptures as a man who had looked at the case against them from the inside. He never forgot what it was to doubt, and he spoke to doubters without contempt.

Minneapolis. His next work was in Minneapolis, where he served as a pastor and as superintendent of the city’s Congregational mission work. There, in 1888, he made a decision that shaped the rest of his life. Having read the life of George Müller of Bristol, who had supported his orphanages by prayer alone, Torrey gave up his salary to work among the poor and resolved to look to God alone for the needs of his family. He had a wife and young children. He later said that from then on their food and clothing came as answers to prayer. The lesson he drew was not that God can be manipulated, but that most Christians stop asking too soon. The habit of praying through, as he called it, never left him.

Moody’s man in Chicago. Torrey had come under the influence of D. L. Moody during a campaign in New Haven, and in 1889 Moody called him to Chicago to be the first superintendent of the Chicago Evangelization Society, the school that became the Moody Bible Institute. He was thirty-three. He built its course of study around the English Bible and practical work, and he sent his students out into the streets, hospitals, jails and tenements of the city. In 1894 he also became pastor of the Chicago Avenue Church, now the Moody Church, and he remained there for twelve years. His best-known little books date from these years: How to Bring Men to Christ, Baptism with the Holy Spirit, What the Bible Teaches, and How to Pray.

The Saturday-night room. In 1898 Torrey began a prayer meeting at the Institute on Saturday evenings. It was not a service. It was an hour of asking, and what they asked for, week after week, was a worldwide outpouring of the Holy Spirit. Torrey prayed privately in those years that God would send him round the world to preach, and not long afterwards an invitation came from Australia. He told the story often, not as a technique but as evidence that God answers.

Grief. The public years had private sorrow. In 1898 the Torreys lost a young daughter to illness. It is worth remembering when his writing seems hard. The man who spoke so confidently of God’s faithfulness had stood at his own child’s grave.

Around the world. From 1902 Torrey travelled with the singer Charles M. Alexander on a series of missions that took them to Australia and New Zealand, to Asia, and through the British Isles. The meetings were enormous. In London in 1905 they filled the Royal Albert Hall day after day for two months. Torrey later remarked that the newspapers kept pointing out that the preacher was no orator, and he agreed with them. He put the crowds down to the uplifted Christ preached in the power of the Spirit, and to the prayers of many thousands of people. He reported the numbers of those who professed faith, but he never claimed them as his own.

The long finishing. Torrey returned to America at the end of 1905, left his Chicago pastorate the following year and his post at the Institute in 1908, and gave himself to campaigns across the country. In 1908 he founded a summer Bible conference at Montrose, Pennsylvania. In 1912 he went west to become the first dean of the Bible Institute of Los Angeles, and from 1915 he was also pastor of the Church of the Open Door there. The sermons collected as The Fundamental Doctrines of the Christian Faith were preached to that congregation. These were also the years of The Fundamentals, the series of volumes defending historic Christianity against the new theology, which he helped to edit. He resigned his Los Angeles posts in 1924 and went back to travelling and preaching.

The end. Torrey wrote more than forty books. He died at his home in Asheville, North Carolina, on the twenty-sixth of October, 1928, at the age of seventy-two, and was buried at Montrose. Those who knew him best did not remember him chiefly for the crowds. They remembered a man of regular, unhurried prayer and daily Bible study, who kept the habits of a small room while he stood before great audiences. The young sceptic who had meant to end his life had promised to go wherever he was sent. He was sent a very long way.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Torrey’s mother prayed for years for a son who scorned her faith. Name someone you have stopped praying for, and begin again today.

2. Torrey took his doubts to their source rather than living with them unexamined. If you have a question about the faith that you have been avoiding, decide how you will honestly look into it.

3. In Minneapolis he learned to pray through rather than give up. Choose one matter you will pray about daily until God answers.

4. The Saturday-night room asked God for things far beyond its own reach. Add one request to your prayers that only God could grant.

5. Choose one of Torrey’s books or sermons in the Ochorus library and read the first chapter this week.

A PRAYER
Lord God, You heard a mother’s prayers for a proud and unhappy son, and You met him when he was ready to die. I thank You that no one is beyond Your reach.
You answered his doubts, supplied his needs and sent him to the ends of the earth. Teach me to trust You as he learned to trust You.
Where I have given up asking, give me courage to ask again. Where I have kept my questions at a distance, give me honesty to face them in Your light.
And make me willing to go where You send me, and to say, Here am I; send me. Amen.

fields.title: A Person, Not an Influence
fields.body_html:
And I will pray the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever; Even the Spirit of truth; whom the world cannot receive, because it seeth him not, neither knoweth him: but ye know him; for he dwelleth with you, and shall be in you. JOHN 14:16–17

Of all the things Torrey taught, the one he thought most basic was this: the Holy Spirit is a Person. He opened both of his larger works on the Spirit with it. The Person and Work of the Holy Spirit begins with a chapter on His personality before a word is said about His work, and The Fundamental Doctrines of the Christian Faith gives the subject a sermon of its own. Torrey’s reason was simple. You cannot understand what someone does until you know who He is. And a great deal of confusion about the Spirit’s work, he thought, came from treating Him as a thing.

Why it matters so much

Torrey put the point in terms of worship, of practice and of experience.

In worship, if the Holy Spirit is a divine Person and we think of Him only as an influence, we are withholding from God the love, trust and adoration that are His due. We would not think of passing a day without thanking the Father for His love or the Son for His sacrifice. How often, Torrey asked, do we thank the Spirit for His?

In practice, the difference is between using and being used. If the Spirit is a power, then our great question will be how to get hold of more of it for our work. If He is a Person, the question turns round. Torrey put it in two sentences that are worth learning by heart. If we think of the Spirit as merely a power, he wrote, our constant thought will be, “How can I get more of the Holy Spirit?” But if we know Him as a divine Person, our thought will rather be, “How can the Holy Spirit have more of me?”

That reversal runs through all of Torrey’s teaching on the Spirit, and it is the key to reading his more controversial chapters rightly. He did not think of the Spirit as fuel for Christian service. He thought of Him as the Lord of it.

But all these worketh that one and the selfsame Spirit, dividing to every man severally as he will. 1 CORINTHIANS 12:11

The marks of a person

Torrey’s method was typical of him. He asked what the marks of personality are, and then looked to see whether Scripture ascribes them to the Spirit. Personality, he said, is not a matter of hands and eyes but of knowing, feeling and willing. Anything that knows, feels and wills is a person.

The Spirit knows. He searches the deep things of God, and no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God.

Many earnest workers, he observed, are struggling to get possession of a mysterious power they can use in their work as they choose. They will never find it, because there is no such power to be had. There is instead a Person, wise as well as mighty, who is willing to take possession of them and use them as He chooses. And Torrey added that we should be glad of it. Imagine what ignorant and sinful people would do with divine power if it were simply handed over to them.

The Spirit loves. Torrey asked his readers to stop over five words in Romans 15:30: the love of the Spirit.

We owe our salvation to that love as truly as to the love of the Father and the Son. It was the Spirit who followed us through years of indifference, who opened our eyes to our need and showed us Christ. Torrey wrote with feeling here, and it is some of his most moving writing.

And the Spirit can be grieved.

One who is grieved

Torrey thought this verse among the most tender in the Bible. The Spirit is not a blind force that we either have or lack. He is a holy Person who lives in the believer, who sees every act, hears every word and knows every thought, and who is grieved by whatever is impure, unkind, selfish or untrue. Torrey compared Him to a godly mother whose son is kept from sin by the thought of how it would wound her if she knew. The Holy Spirit is holier than any mother and loves more than any mother, and He does not need to be told. Of this truth Torrey wrote, “I know of no thought that will help one more than this to lead a holy life and to walk softly in the presence of the Holy One.”

Acts only a person can do

Torrey went on to show that Scripture ascribes to the Spirit acts that only a person performs. He teaches and brings to remembrance. He speaks, and says, Separate me Barnabas and Saul. He intercedes for us with groanings which cannot be uttered. He can be lied to, as Ananias found, and to lie to the Holy Ghost, Peter says, is to lie to God.

Howbeit when he, the Spirit of truth, is come, he will guide you into all truth: for he shall not speak of himself; but whatsoever he shall hear, that shall he speak: and he will shew you things to come. JOHN 16:13

Torrey’s arguments here are sound and they have stood the test of time. The only caution is one he himself would have accepted. It is possible to prove the personality of the Spirit, as he does, by a careful catalogue of texts, and still not know Him. Torrey’s real point was not intellectual. It was that thousands of Christians, as he testified, found their whole experience transformed when they began to treat the Spirit as a real and present Friend. He also wrote, and it is worth hearing, that a wrong idea of the Spirit as a power to be possessed tends to make people proud, and that the true idea makes them humble. “I can think of no thought more humbling or more overwhelming,” he wrote, “than the thought that a person of Divine majesty and glory dwells in my heart and is ready to use me.” Anyone who finds that talk of the Spirit is making him feel superior to other Christians has probably lost sight of the Person.

The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all. Amen. 2 CORINTHIANS 13:14

fields.title: The Baptism with the Holy Spirit
fields.body_html:
But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judæa, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth. ACTS 1:8

No subject is more closely tied to Torrey’s name than this one. He wrote a small book on it, Baptism with the Holy Spirit, gave it a chapter in How to Bring Men to Christ and another in The Person and Work of the Holy Spirit, and preached it in almost every campaign. It is also the part of his teaching that has been most argued over. This chapter sets out what he taught. The next two follow him into how the blessing is received and how it is kept, and all three say where he needs to be weighed.

What it is not

The baptism with the Spirit, he said, is not regeneration. The apostles were already clean through the word Christ had spoken to them, and yet He told them they would be baptised with the Holy Ghost not many days hence. The believers at Samaria had received the word of God and been baptised in water, and still Peter and John prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Ghost.

Who, when they were come down, prayed for them, that they might receive the Holy Ghost: (For as yet he was fallen upon none of them: only they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus.) ACTS 8:15–16

From passages like these Torrey concluded that a person may be truly born again and not yet baptised with the Spirit. The Spirit dwells in every believer, he insisted — without Him no one belongs to Christ at all — but the baptism is something further.

Nor, and this is important, is it the removal of the sinful nature. Here Torrey parted company with some of the holiness teachers of his day, who taught that a second blessing after conversion eradicates inbred sin. He agreed that there is a further experience and that it may be received at once, but he flatly denied that it cleanses the heart from sin. “The Baptism with the Holy Spirit is not to cleanse from sin,” he wrote, “but to empower for service.” Victory over sin is indeed the Spirit’s work, but it is a daily walk, maintained moment by moment, not a single crisis.

What it is

Positively, Torrey defined the baptism in terms of Acts 1:8. It is power for witness and service. Every passage in which it is mentioned, he argued, connects it with testimony and work. His own summary is careful and worth quoting whole: “The Baptism with the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of God coming upon the believer, taking possession of his faculties, imparting to him gifts not naturally his own, but which qualify him for the service to which God has called him.”

And, behold, I send the promise of my Father upon you: but tarry ye in the city of Jerusalem, until ye be endued with power from on high. LUKE 24:49

He held that it is a definite experience, one of which a person can say yes or no. Paul asked the disciples at Ephesus whether they had received the Holy Ghost since they believed, and he expected a plain answer.

He said unto them, Have ye received the Holy Ghost since ye believed? And they said unto him, We have not so much as heard whether there be any Holy Ghost. ACTS 19:2

And he held that it is for every believer. Peter said the promise was for his hearers, for their children, and for all that are afar off. Torrey took that as reaching down to his own day and to every reader.

Not the same in everyone

One of the wisest parts of Torrey’s teaching is his insistence that the power does not look the same in every life. He confessed that in his early study he had wondered whether everyone baptised with the Spirit would speak in tongues, and was set right by Paul’s question, do all speak with tongues? Then he fell into a second error, supposing that the baptism would make everyone a preacher or evangelist. First Corinthians 12 cured him of that too.

Now there are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit. 1 CORINTHIANS 12:4

He named three evils that come from the mistake. The first is disappointment: people seek power as evangelists when God has not called them to be evangelists, and are left in despair. The second is presumption: a man rushes into preaching because he thinks the Spirit is all he needs, when he also needs a call and a knowledge of the Word. The third, and worst, is indifference: the mother of a large family concludes that since she is not called to preach, the whole matter is nothing to her. But she, Torrey said, needs the Spirit’s power for the holy work of bringing up her children as much as any preacher needs it for the pulpit. He told of a mother who, after receiving this blessing, found she could reach her children’s hearts as never before.

The necessity

Torrey pressed the necessity of this blessing in the strongest terms. The apostles had been with Christ for three years, had heard His teaching and seen His resurrection, and still they were told to wait. Jesus Himself did not begin His public ministry until the Spirit had come upon Him at the Jordan.

How God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Ghost and with power: who went about doing good, and healing all that were oppressed of the devil; for God was with him. ACTS 10:38

If that was so for them, Torrey argued, what is it for us to go on without it? There is nothing more deadly, he wrote, than the gospel without the Spirit’s power. A preacher can say every true thing and say it in the energy of the flesh.

And my speech and my preaching was not with enticing words of man’s wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power. 1 CORINTHIANS 2:4

Weighing it

Here the reader must think carefully, because good Christians have disagreed.

Much of what Torrey taught is plainly right. Service for Christ needs the power of the Spirit and not merely training. The Spirit is sovereign in His gifts. Many Christians are working in their own strength, and they ought to ask God for His. None of that depends on Torrey’s particular scheme.

What is disputed is the scheme itself: that there is one definite experience, called the baptism, which normally comes after conversion and which a believer may lack for years. Many careful readers point out that Paul uses the language of baptism for what happens to every Christian at the start.

For by one Spirit are we all baptized into one body, whether we be Jews or Gentiles, whether we be bond or free; and have been all made to drink into one Spirit. 1 CORINTHIANS 12:13

On this reading, the Samaritan and Ephesian cases in Acts belong to a unique moment in the spread of the gospel, and what believers need afterwards is not a second baptism but to be filled with the Spirit again and again, as Ephesians 5:18 commands. Torrey himself insisted on repeated fillings, as the next chapters will show, so the two views are nearer in practice than in vocabulary.

It should also be said that Torrey’s language was later taken up by movements whose teaching he did not share, especially on tongues as the necessary sign. His own book is clear that tongues are not the sign, and that the power shows itself as the Spirit wills.

The safest course is to hold firmly what is certain and lightly what is argued. It is certain that we need the Spirit’s power, that God gives the Spirit to them that ask Him, and that the power is for witness. Whether you call your own experience of that power a baptism or a filling matters much less than whether you have sought it.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Ask yourself honestly whether your Christian service — at home, at work, in church — is being done in your own strength or in the Spirit’s.

2. Reflect on the three evils Torrey named. Which of them — disappointment, presumption or indifference — is nearest to you?

3. Put yourself deliberately at the Spirit’s disposal for whatever service He chooses, rather than asking Him to bless the service you have chosen.

4. Read 1 Corinthians 12 slowly this week and note the variety of the Spirit’s gifts.

5. Read the first chapter of Torrey’s Baptism with the Holy Spirit in the Ochorus library, and weigh it against 1 Corinthians 12:13 and Ephesians 5:18.

A PRAYER
Father, Your Son promised that His disciples would receive power when the Holy Ghost came upon them. I confess how much of my service has been done without that power.
I do not ask for a gift of my own choosing or a field of my own planning. I put myself at Your disposal.
Fill me with Your Spirit, that I may witness to Jesus Christ in the place where You have set me, with the gifts You choose to give.
Keep me from pride if You use me, and from despair if You use me differently than I hoped. Amen.

fields.title: How Much More Shall Your Father Give
fields.body_html:
If ye then, being evil, know how to give good gifts unto your children: how much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him? LUKE 11:13

Having persuaded his readers that they needed the power of the Spirit, Torrey did what he always did. He told them how to get it. The third chapter of Baptism with the Holy Spirit sets out seven steps, all of them found or implied, he said, in Peter’s answer on the day of Pentecost.

Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost. ACTS 2:38

It is characteristic Torrey: definite, numbered, practical and supremely confident. He believed that whoever took these steps would with absolute certainty enter the blessing, because the Word of God was equally positive. We will follow the steps first and weigh the confidence afterwards.

Turning to Christ and from sin

The first two steps are found in the word repent. Torrey took repentance to mean a change of mind, and first of all a change of mind about Jesus. Peter’s hearers had crucified the One whom God had made both Lord and Christ. To repent was to accept Him as Lord and Christ. So the first step is to accept Jesus as Christ and Lord.

The second step is a change of mind about sin: to renounce it, all of it. Torrey thought this the commonest hindrance of all. Something is held on to that we feel, more or less definitely, does not please God. We cannot search our own hearts thoroughly enough, he said; God must do it. So we should go alone with Him and ask Him to search us, and wait for Him to bring to light whatever is wrong, and put it away at once.

Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts: And see if there be any wicked way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting. PSALM 139:23–24

Confession and surrender

The third step is open confession. Peter said, be baptised. Torrey saw in Christ’s own baptism, after which the Spirit descended on Him, a pattern: humbling oneself to take the sinner’s place openly. The Spirit is not for the secret disciple but for the one who confesses Christ publicly. He acknowledged exceptions, such as Cornelius’s household, and he did not deny that Christians who do not practise water baptism have known the Spirit’s power, but he held that the passage gives the normal order.

The fourth step is obedience, and here Torrey meant something deep.

And we are his witnesses of these things; and so is also the Holy Ghost, whom God hath given to them that obey him. ACTS 5:32

The fifth step is real desire. The asking Jesus speaks of in Luke 11 comes straight after the parable of the friend at midnight, and it is not the asking of a passing wish. Torrey turned to Isaiah’s promise of water on the thirsty. When a man is really thirsty, he said, he has only one cry.

The seventh step is faith. Here Torrey drew on two texts that shaped his whole doctrine of prayer.

And this is the confidence that we have in him, that, if we ask any thing according to his will, he heareth us: And if we know that he hear us, whatsoever we ask, we know that we have the petitions that we desired of him. 1 JOHN 5:14–15

His reasoning was straightforward. The gift of the Spirit is plainly promised, so to ask for it is to ask according to God’s will. Such a prayer is heard. If it is heard, we have what we asked. So the one who has met the conditions and asked may rise from his knees and say, on the authority of God’s Word, that he has received, and go to his work expecting the power. There is a great deal here that every Christian needs. Christ must be Lord. Sin must be dealt with honestly. The will must be surrendered. Desire must be real and motives pure. God does give the Holy Spirit to them that ask Him, and faith does rest on His word rather than on feelings. A reader could take any one of these steps this week and be the better for it.

The danger lies in the certainty of the formula. Torrey wrote as though anyone who had met seven conditions could know, as surely as a sum adds up, that he had received a specific experience. That can help a timid believer to trust God’s promise. It can also turn the gift of God into a technique, and send a sensitive conscience round and round the list asking which step it has failed. fields.body_html:
And when they had prayed, the place was shaken where they were assembled together; and they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and they spake the word of God with boldness. ACTS 4:31

Torrey’s teaching on the baptism with the Spirit is often remembered as if it described a single event that settles everything. He did not teach that. The last two chapters of Baptism with the Holy Spirit are among the most sober things he wrote. One is about the need to be filled again and again. The other is about how spiritual power is lost. Taken together they correct any idea that one experience, however real, can carry a believer through a lifetime.

Peter, filled three times

Torrey noticed something about Peter. He was among those filled with the Holy Ghost on the day of Pentecost. Shortly afterwards, standing before the rulers, he was filled again.

Then Peter, filled with the Holy Ghost, said unto them, Ye rulers of the people, and elders of Israel. ACTS 4:8

And a little later, when the believers prayed after the apostles were released, the place was shaken and they were all filled with the Holy Ghost — Peter among them. Three fillings in a few chapters.

From this Torrey drew a plain lesson: “As new emergencies of service arise, there must be new fillings with the Spirit.” He thought that a failure to grasp this explained a sad sight he had seen many times — men who had once plainly worked in the Spirit’s power and now showed little sign of it, because they were trying to live on an experience from years before. For each new day, each new piece of service, each person to be dealt with, he urged believers to ask definitely for a fresh filling.

He was careful with words here. Since Scripture uses the phrase baptised with the Holy Spirit only of the first experience, and since the word baptism itself suggests a beginning, he thought it wisest to speak of later experiences as fillings rather than fresh baptisms. Those who disagree with his view of a second blessing will find this chapter the place where they agree with him most. Whatever the first experience is called, the command of Scripture is continuous.

And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit. EPHESIANS 5:18

How power is lost

The last chapter of the book opens with Samson. Time and again the Spirit of the Lord came upon him, and then came the terrible verse.

And he awoke out of his sleep, and said, I will go out as at other times before, and shake myself. And he wist not that the LORD was departed from him. JUDGES 16:20

Torrey thought there had been many Samsons, and would be many more: people whom God had once used and then had to lay aside. He named seven ways in which power is lost, and they are worth setting out plainly.

The first is going back on one’s separation to God. Samson’s uncut hair was the sign of his vow. When it was shorn, his separation was gone, and his strength with it. So a Christian who once turned his back on the world and gave himself wholly to God may let the world win his heart again, and the power goes. The remedy, Torrey said, is to let the hair grow again: renew the dedication.

The second is the incoming of sin. Saul began with the Spirit of God upon him and a great victory, and ended in ruin because he disobeyed.

But the Spirit of the LORD departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the LORD troubled him. 1 SAMUEL 16:14

The one who would keep God’s power, Torrey wrote, must walk very softly before Him and respond promptly to His slightest whisper. He recommended going alone with God at the close of each day to ask whether anything displeasing had crept in, and confessing it then and there. David sinned grievously, and when he confessed, he knew the Spirit’s power again.

The third is self-indulgence. There are things not sinful in themselves that dull spirituality and rob men of power. Torrey did not believe anyone could live luxuriously, indulge his appetites freely and know the fulness of God’s power. He saw it happen to preachers: popularity brought comfort, comfort brought luxury, and the Spirit’s power went out as the luxury came in. “I frankly confess I am afraid of luxury,” he wrote; “not as afraid of it as I am of sin, but it comes next as an object of dread.”

Thou therefore endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ. 2 TIMOTHY 2:3

The fourth is greed for money. It was the love of accumulating that got into the heart of Judas. Torrey observed that a poor man can be as absorbed in the desire for wealth as any millionaire.

And he said unto them, Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man’s life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth. LUKE 12:15

The fifth, and he thought the most deceptive and dangerous of all, is pride. Men who have never gone back on their dedication, never let conscious sin in, never grown luxurious or greedy, fail at last because God has used them and they have become proud of it. God cannot use a proud man, Torrey said, and God resists the proud. Even Moses, the meekest of men, failed here at the rock. If God is using us at all, let us get down very low before Him.

Likewise, ye younger, submit yourselves unto the elder. Yea, all of you be subject one to another, and be clothed with humility: for God resisteth the proud, and giveth grace to the humble. 1 PETER 5:5

The sixth is neglect of prayer, and the seventh is neglect of the Word. Power flows out in service and must be renewed in prayer. It comes through meditation on Scripture, and when business and even Christian duties crowd the Word out, many a man has run dry.

Fear and assurance

The chapter ends with one of Torrey’s most personal passages. “If there is one fear that comes to me more frequently than any other,” he wrote, “it is that of losing the power of God.” He could not imagine anything worse than to have been used by God and then laid aside, to see a perishing world and know there was no power in one’s words to save.

But in the same breath he drew a distinction that is vital. “I have little fear of losing eternal life,” he wrote. Every believer has that already, held in the hand of Christ and of the Father. What may be lost is not salvation but usefulness.

And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand. JOHN 10:28

It must also be said that not every loss of fruitfulness is a sign of hidden sin. There are seasons when God sends His servants into hidden places, into sickness, obscurity or apparent failure, for reasons He does not explain. Torrey’s list is a searching mirror to hold up in prayer, but it is not a rule for judging others whose ministry has dimmed.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Before your next piece of service — a conversation, a lesson, a hard task at home — ask God specifically to fill you with His Spirit for it.

2. Go through Torrey’s seven ways in which power is lost. Mark the one you are most in danger of, and bring it honestly to God.

3. Establish a short time at the end of each day to ask God to show you anything displeasing to Him, and to confess it.

4. Look at your spending and comforts this month. Is there any area of luxury that is dulling your spiritual life?

5. If God has used you in any way recently, thank Him for it, and ask Him to keep you from pride.

A PRAYER
Lord, I do not want to live on yesterday’s blessing. Fill me with Your Spirit today, and again tomorrow, and for every task You give me.
Keep me from the things that make You withdraw Your hand: from going back on my dedication, from sin, from luxury, from greed, from pride, and from neglect of prayer and of Your Word.
If You have used me, keep me low before You. If I have grown careless, bring me back.
And thank You that, whatever my usefulness, I am held in the hand of Christ, and no one can take me out of it. Amen.

fields.title: The Law of the Spirit of Life
fields.body_html:
For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus hath made me free from the law of sin and death. ROMANS 8:2

Torrey insisted that the baptism with the Spirit is for service, not for cleansing from sin. But he did not therefore think the Spirit had nothing to do with holiness. Quite the reverse. In The Person and Work of the Holy Spirit he gives a series of chapters to what the Spirit does within the believer: setting him free from the power of indwelling sin, forming Christ within him, bearing the fruit of Christlike character, guiding him as a son, and bearing witness that he is a child of God. This is the inner side of Torrey’s teaching on the Spirit, and in some ways the most helpful.

Three laws

Torrey read Romans 7 and 8 as a story of three laws. There is the law of God outside us, holy and just and good, which Paul approved in his mind. There is the law of sin within, which kept saying, in effect, you cannot do the good you want. And the battle between them ended in defeat.

O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death? I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord. ROMANS 7:24–25

Then Paul discovered a third law, the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus. What the law of God could not do, because it was weak through the flesh, the Spirit could do in him: fulfil the righteousness the law requires in those who walk after the Spirit.

That the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit. ROMANS 8:4

Torrey’s practical point was this. When we come to the end of ourselves, admit our inability to keep God’s law, and look in helplessness to the Spirit to do what we cannot, surrendering our thoughts and desires to Him, He sets us free from the power of the sin that dwells in us. It is the privilege of the child of God, Torrey wrote, to have victory over sin every day, every hour and every moment.

The flesh still there

It is important to hear what Torrey did not say. He did not teach that the believer’s sinful nature is removed. The desires of the flesh remain. What changes is that we are no longer in the flesh or living after it. Through the Spirit we put to death, day by day, the deeds to which those desires would lead.

For if ye live after the flesh, ye shall die: but if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live. ROMANS 8:13

Torrey wrote that the Spirit’s power may be so full that a believer is hardly conscious of the flesh at all; it may seem dead and gone. But it is only kept in the place of death by the Holy Spirit. If we took our eyes off Christ, or neglected the Word and prayer, down we would go.

This I say then, Walk in the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfil the lust of the flesh. GALATIANS 5:16

He told of a man he had known who made extraordinary progress and became a teacher of thousands, and who seemed to Torrey to be growing self-confident. Torrey invited him to his room and warned him frankly. He found it safer himself, he said, not to be too sure at the end of each day that there had been no failures, but to ask God to search his heart. It is a wise word from a man who could otherwise sound very confident.

Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall. 1 CORINTHIANS 10:12

Christ formed within

The next step in Torrey’s thought comes from Paul’s prayer in Ephesians 3.

That he would grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with might by his Spirit in the inner man; That Christ may dwell in your hearts by faith. EPHESIANS 3:16–17

In Christ on the cross, Torrey said, we have Christ for us. By the Spirit we have Christ in us, and there lies the secret of a Christlike life. Torrey then turned to Romans 8:14. As many as are led by the Spirit of God, they are the sons of God. “A true Christian life,” he wrote, “is a personally conducted life, conducted at every turn by a Divine Person.”

This led him to one of his most liberating emphases. Many Christians, he observed, live in bondage to long lists of rules they have made for themselves. The Christian is not governed by rules outside him but led by the Spirit of adoption within. And if he goes astray in a thoughtless moment, he does not fall into terror. He goes to his Father, confesses, believes he is forgiven because God says so, and goes on light-hearted.

fields.body_html:
Ye lust, and have not: ye kill, and desire to have, and cannot obtain: ye fight and war, yet ye have not, because ye ask not. JAMES 4:2

If Torrey is remembered for one book above the rest, it is How to Pray. It is a short work, plain and practical, and it has been reprinted for more than a century. It is not in the Ochorus library, but its teaching runs through the books that are, especially the chapter on prayer in How to Succeed in the Christian Life, and through the story of his own life. Torrey was not a theorist of prayer. He had given up his salary in Minneapolis and watched his family fed in answer to it. He had led a room of hundreds in asking for revival on Saturday nights. When he wrote about prayer, he was reporting what he had proved.

Ye have not because ye ask not

Torrey began with the plainest of diagnoses. Very much of the failure in Christian living and Christian work, he wrote in How to Succeed in the Christian Life, comes from the neglect of prayer. Why do I make so little headway? Why have I so little victory over sin? Why do I accomplish so little? God answers through James: ye have not, because ye ask not.

An audience with the King

The heart of Torrey’s teaching on prayer is not technique but the sense of whom we are addressing. In How to Pray he urged that before we ask for anything we should take time to realise that we are actually in the presence of God, and speaking to Him. Much so-called prayer, he thought, is spoken into the air, with the mind on the request rather than on the One to whom it is made.

In How to Succeed in the Christian Life he put it through a picture. Prayer is an audience with the King. A subject summoned to the king never asks how much time he must spend with him, but how much time the king will give him. So the question of the Christian should not be, How much time must I spend in prayer? but, How much time may I spend in prayer, with due regard to other duties?

Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need. HEBREWS 4:16

That is the right place to start. Duty alone will not keep anyone praying for long. The privilege of being heard by God will.

Set times

Torrey was practical about the shape of a praying life. He commended the rule of David and of Daniel: three times a day.

Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray, and cry aloud: and he shall hear my voice. PSALM 55:17

He knew that one can pray while walking the street or sitting at a desk, and he wanted Christians to learn to lift their hearts to God in the busiest moments. “It is not needful to be on your knees all the time,” he wrote, “but the heart should be on its knees all the time.” But he insisted that there must also be set times, when we go alone with God and shut the door.

But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly. MATTHEW 6:6

Fighting battles before they come

His counsel for the morning is one of the most useful things he wrote. Begin the day with thanksgiving for definite mercies and prayer for definite needs. Then think ahead to the temptations the day is likely to bring, and ask God for strength to overcome them before they arrive. Many fail in the battle, Torrey observed, because they wait until the hour of battle. Others succeed because they have won the victory on their knees beforehand.

And he gave a rule for busy days that sounds absurd until it is tried: the more work a day holds, the more time must be given to prayer in preparation for it. “Prayer is the greatest time saver known to man,” he wrote. In How to Bring Men to Christ he said the same of Christian work: by praying more we will not work any less, and we will accomplish vastly more.

A clean balance sheet

At midday he recommended a few minutes alone with God to keep calm amid the anxieties of the day. And at night he urged two things.

The first is thanksgiving in detail. Review the blessings of the day and thank God for each. Nothing, he said, increases faith more than a calm review each evening of what God has done, and nothing brings larger blessings than intelligent thanks for those already given.

The second is confession. Ask God to show you anything in the day that displeased Him. Wait quietly, and listen. Confess what He shows you, frankly, as to a loving Father, and believe that He forgives it, because He says He does.

If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. 1 JOHN 1:9

Torrey compared it to a bank that never closes its day until its balance is correct. Do this, he wrote, “and you can never backslide for more than twenty-four hours.” It is a characteristic sentence — confident, practical and very nearly true. Accounts left crooked for months are hard to straighten. Accounts settled every night are not.

Praying together

Torrey did not think private prayer was enough. He urged every Christian to attend the prayer meeting of his church, to guard that night from other engagements, and, if the meeting was a prayer meeting in name only, quietly to work to make it real. He also commended praying regularly with a small company of like-minded friends. His own Saturday-night meeting at the Institute was the living example. He believed that revival comes in answer to united, persevering prayer, and that the world tour which followed was the harvest of that room.

Three things to ask for

Finally, he named three things that anyone who would succeed in the Christian life must pray for especially: wisdom, strength, and the Holy Spirit.

But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint. ISAIAH 40:31

Torrey’s approach can feel mechanical to some readers, with its times and rules and balance sheets. He would have said that the rules are scaffolding, and that the building is fellowship with the Father. He was right to insist on both. Unstructured good intentions rarely become a life of prayer. Structures without the sense of the King’s presence rarely stay alive. Keep the structure, and remember whom you are speaking to.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Ask yourself honestly how much time you spent in prayer last week. Then ask how much time you would give to an audience with a king.

2. Choose set times for prayer — at least morning and evening — and keep them for a month.

3. Tomorrow morning, think ahead to the temptations of the day and pray through them before they come.

4. On your busiest day this week, deliberately give more time to prayer beforehand, and notice what happens.

5. Tonight, review the day with thanksgiving in detail, ask God to show you anything displeasing to Him, and settle the account before you sleep.

A PRAYER
Lord, teach me to pray. I confess that I have not because I ask not, and that I have looked for every explanation of my weakness but the true one.
Let me come to You as a subject summoned before the King, glad of every moment You give me.
Meet me in the morning before the battles of the day, keep my heart on its knees through the busy hours, and settle my account with You each night.
And give me wisdom, strength and Your Holy Spirit, for Jesus’ sake. Amen.

fields.title: Praying in the Holy Ghost
fields.body_html:
But ye, beloved, building up yourselves on your most holy faith, praying in the Holy Ghost. JUDE 1:20

The last chapter was about the habits of prayer. This one is about its inner secret. Torrey believed that God answers prayer — not in a vague sense, but definitely, specifically and in ways that can be recognised. He also believed that there are conditions to prevailing prayer, and that the deepest of them is that the prayer be prayed in the Holy Spirit. His chapter on the subject in The Person and Work of the Holy Spirit is short, and it is one of the best things he wrote.

We know not what we should pray for

Torrey started from our ignorance. The disciples did not know how to pray, and asked Jesus to teach them. We are no different. We do not know what to pray for, or how to ask for it. “There is no place where we need to recognize our ignorance more than we do in prayer,” he wrote.

Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities: for we know not what we should pray for as we ought: but the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered. ROMANS 8:26

But there is One always at hand who does know. True prayer, Torrey said, is prayer in the Spirit: the prayer that the Spirit inspires and directs. And the prayer He directs is prayer according to the will of God.

And he that searcheth the hearts knoweth what is the mind of the Spirit, because he maketh intercession for the saints according to the will of God. ROMANS 8:27

This led him to a sentence that sums up his whole doctrine: “The prayer that God, the Holy Spirit, inspires is the prayer that God, the Father, answers.”

Not bending God to our will

Torrey was aware of an objection. Some people thought the Christian doctrine of prayer meant that ignorant human beings could go to God and change His will, subjecting His wisdom to their foolishness. That, he said, is not the Christian doctrine at all. The Christian doctrine is that the believer may be taught by the Spirit what the will of God is, and so be led to ask not for what our foolishness would suggest, but for what the Spirit prompts.

How do we know the will of God? First, Torrey said, by what is written. Every promise in the Bible is sure, and if God has promised something, we may be certain it is His will to give it. Second, where there is no specific promise, the Spirit Himself may lead us, sometimes clearly and sometimes in longings too deep for words, which God understands even if we do not.

Now unto him that is able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think, according to the power that worketh in us. EPHESIANS 3:20

The confidence of faith

Once the will of God is known, Torrey held, faith can be definite. He told how the strange tenses of Mark 11:24 had long confused him, until the answer came to him while studying John’s first epistle.

And this is the confidence that we have in him, that, if we ask any thing according to his will, he heareth us: And if we know that he hear us, whatsoever we ask, we know that we have the petitions that we desired of him. 1 JOHN 5:14–15

If I know the prayer is according to God’s will, I know it is heard. If it is heard, I have the petition, even if I do not yet see it. That was how he came to understand the words believe that ye receive them, and ye shall have them. It was the confidence that let him rise from his knees and go to his work expecting the answer.

Conditions of prevailing prayer

Torrey did not think every prayer was answered simply because it was sincere. In How to Pray and elsewhere he set out conditions drawn from Scripture, and they are searching.

Prayer is to be made in the name of Christ — not as a formula at the end, but resting entirely on His merit and claims.

And whatsoever ye shall ask in my name, that will I do, that the Father may be glorified in the Son. JOHN 14:13

It depends on abiding in Christ and letting His words abide in us.

If ye abide in me, and my words abide in you, ye shall ask what ye will, and it shall be done unto you. JOHN 15:7

It depends on obedience. Unconfessed sin shuts the door, and cherished iniquity closes God’s ear.

If I regard iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear me. PSALM 66:18

And it requires persistence.

Praying through

Torrey learned from George Müller, whose life he had read, the habit of persevering in prayer until the answer came. He called it praying through. The parables of the friend at midnight and the unjust judge were for him not puzzles but commands.

And he spake a parable unto them to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint. LUKE 18:1

He believed that many prayers fail not because God refuses, but because we stop asking too soon. We pray once or twice, grow discouraged and move on. The friend at midnight received what he needed because of his importunity. Torrey did not think this meant God is reluctant and must be worn down. He thought it meant that persevering prayer tests and deepens our desire, and brings us into line with God’s will, and that God delights to answer the one who will not let Him go.

Where care is needed

There is much here to embrace. There is also a danger, and it is the same as with his teaching on the baptism with the Spirit.

It is possible to take believe that ye receive them as a method for obtaining whatever we want, and to decide in advance that because we have asked with enough faith the thing must be ours. Torrey guarded against this by insisting that the prayer be according to God’s will, and by teaching that we must wait on the Spirit to know it. But his confident manner can hide those safeguards from a hasty reader.

Scripture shows us prayers that were not answered in the way they were asked. Paul besought the Lord three times for his thorn to be removed, and was given grace instead.

For this thing I besought the Lord thrice, that it might depart from me. And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. 2 CORINTHIANS 12:8–9

And the Son of God Himself prayed in Gethsemane, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt. No one prayed more perfectly in the Spirit than He did. The answer was the cross, and through the cross, the resurrection.

So pray definitely. Pray boldly. Pray through. But let the Spirit teach you what to ask, and hold every request, as Jesus did, within not my will but Thine.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Next time you pray, begin by confessing your ignorance of what to ask, and wait quietly for the Spirit to lead your desires before you speak.

2. Find one promise of God that applies to a present need. Pray it back to Him, and thank Him that He has heard.

3. Ask whether there is any sin you are regarding in your heart that may be hindering your prayers. Deal with it today.

4. Choose one long-standing request and resolve to pray through: to keep asking daily until God answers or makes His will plain.

5. Where a prayer has not been answered as you hoped, read 2 Corinthians 12:7–10 and ask whether God is offering grace instead.

A PRAYER
Holy Spirit, I do not know what I should pray for as I ought. Teach me to pray.

We do not know what to pray for, or how to ask for it. “There is no place where we need to recognize our ignorance more than we do in prayer,” he wrote. Find one promise of God that applies to a present need. Pray it back to Him, and thank Him that He has heard. 3. Ask whether there is any sin you are regarding in your heart that may be hindering your prayers. Deal with it today. 4. fields.body_html:
As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby. 1 PETER 2:2

Torrey spent his working life teaching people to read the Bible. He ran a Bible institute for nearly twenty years and led another, wrote How to Study the Bible for Greatest Profit and What the Bible Teaches, and gave a long chapter to Bible study in How to Succeed in the Christian Life. His conviction was simple: “The soul’s proper food is found in one book, the Bible.” A Christian who neglects it will fail. A Christian who studies it rightly will grow.

Feeding yourself

Torrey began with an analogy. Physical health depends on what we eat and how much. So does spiritual health. A good minister will feed his people on the Word, but he feeds them once or twice a week, and we need to eat every day. More than that, we must learn to feed ourselves. Torrey thought this was also the believer’s best protection. In a day when false teaching abounds, he wrote, the only Christian who is safe from error is the one who studies the Bible for himself. Paul, leaving the Ephesian elders to face grievous wolves, commended them to God and to the word of His grace.

And now, brethren, I commend you to God, and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up, and to give you an inheritance among all them which are sanctified. ACTS 20:32

Daily, and at the best hour

His first rule was daily study. The Bereans searched the Scriptures daily, and Torrey said that after more than a quarter of a century as a Christian he still would not dare let a single day pass without listening to God’s voice in His Book.

These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so. ACTS 17:11

He quoted Moody with approval: in prayer we talk to God, in Bible study God talks to us, and we had better let God do most of the talking. And he gave a practical minimum. No one ought to give less than fifteen minutes a day, he said, and he set the figure deliberately low so that no young Christian would be discouraged. Many busy people he knew gave an hour, some two.

Systematically and thoroughly

Torrey disliked random reading. He suggested that a young Christian begin with John’s Gospel, reading it through five times, then Luke five times, then Acts, 1 Thessalonians, 1 John, Romans and Ephesians in the same way. After that the reader could go through the Bible chapter by chapter, asking of each: what is its principal subject? what truth does it most emphasise? what is its best lesson and its best verse? who are its people? and what does it teach about Jesus Christ?

For the most important chapters he offered a longer method, ending with two questions worth keeping for life. What truth already known has come to me with new power? And what definite thing have I resolved to do as a result of this chapter?

Thoughtfully

Torrey told of a busy man hurrying for a train who asked him to say in a word how to study the Bible. His reply was one word: “Thoughtfully.”

He meant it. The Bible has no magic power, he wrote; it does good only by the truth it contains. “It is better to read one verse attentively than to read a dozen chapters thoughtlessly.” When a verse takes hold of you, stop and ponder it. Mark what impresses you. Memorise the passages that move you most, and learn where they are found.

Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee. PSALM 119:11

He urged comparing Scripture with Scripture. “The best commentary on the Bible is the Bible itself,” he wrote, and he recommended a book of cross-references to help. A difficult passage, he believed, is always explained somewhere else.

Believingly

His most important rule was to study the Bible as what it is: the Word of God.

For this cause also thank we God without ceasing, because, when ye received the word of God which ye heard of us, ye received it not as the word of men, but as it is in truth, the word of God, which effectually worketh also in you that believe. 1 THESSALONIANS 2:13

People sometimes say we should study the Bible like any other book. Torrey granted that the ordinary rules of grammar and language apply, but he insisted that the Bible is unique and must be studied as no other book is. That means an eagerness to find out exactly what it says, a readiness to accept what it teaches even when it seems strange to us, and a practical obedience to it. A child who dismisses his wise father’s statements because they seem unreasonable, Torrey said, is not a philosopher but a fool; and the greatest human mind is an infant beside God.

With the Teacher

Finally, Torrey insisted that the Bible must be studied prayerfully, looking to its Author to explain it. In The Person and Work of the Holy Spirit he gave a whole chapter to the Spirit as Teacher.

But the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my name, he shall teach you all things, and bring all things to your remembrance, whatsoever I have said unto you. JOHN 14:26

He told of a man of thirty-two, long in business, who came to him in tears because he could not memorise Scripture and thought he must give up his training for Christian work. Torrey told him to learn one passage at a time and trust the Spirit to bring it to mind when needed. The man went on to work in a hard field, where opponents gathered round him in the street, and he found that the Scriptures he needed came to him.

Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law. PSALM 119:18

A word of balance

Torrey’s methods have helped a great many people, and they can be taken up as they stand. Two cautions are worth adding. The first is that methods are servants. His numbered questions are excellent, but the goal is not to fill in a form. It is to hear God. The second is that his confidence that every difficulty is explained elsewhere in Scripture, while it expresses a sound instinct — Scripture does interpret Scripture — can be pressed too far. Some things in the Bible remain hard, and it is no failure of faith to say so. That is the subject of the next chapter.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Decide on a set time each day for Bible study, preferably early, and never less than fifteen minutes. Keep it for a month.

2. If you are young in faith, begin with John’s Gospel and read it through several times.

3. Take one chapter this week and ask Torrey’s questions of it, ending with: what definite thing will I do as a result?

4. Memorise one verse that moves you this week, together with its reference.

5. Before you open the Bible each day, ask the Holy Spirit to open your eyes and teach you.

A PRAYER
Lord, You have given me Your Word as the food of my soul, and I have often gone hungry by my own neglect.
Give me an appetite for it, as a newborn child desires milk. Teach me to read it daily, thoughtfully, and as Your own voice.
Holy Spirit, You are the Author of the Book. Open my eyes, bring its words to my remembrance, and make me a doer and not a hearer only.
Let me hide Your word in my heart, that I might not sin against You. Amen.

fields.title: The Scripture Cannot Be Broken
fields.body_html:
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness: That the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works. 2 TIMOTHY 3:16–17

Torrey had once been a clever young critic of the Bible. He knew the arguments against it from the inside, and he had gone to Germany to hear them from their masters. That history gives weight to what he later taught about Scripture. He was not a man who had never looked at the questions. He was a man who had looked hard and come to the opposite conclusion. The first sermon in The Fundamental Doctrines of the Christian Faith is on inspiration, and How to Succeed in the Christian Life has a chapter on difficulties in the Bible. Together they give his view of the Book.

What the Bible claims

Torrey framed the question sharply. Either the writers of Scripture were so taught and governed by the Holy Spirit that what they wrote was true and without error, or they were inspired only in the loose sense in which men of genius are said to be inspired. If the first, we have a final court of appeal on every question of doctrine and duty. If the second, we are at sea, and every generation must guess what the Spirit meant to say through fallible reporters.

For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost. 2 PETER 1:21

He then set out what Scripture claims for itself. The Spirit’s work in prophets and apostles, he argued from 1 Corinthians 12, differed in kind and not merely in degree from His work in other believers. Truth hidden for ages was revealed to them. And the Spirit gave not only the thoughts but the words.

Which things also we speak, not in the words which man’s wisdom teacheth, but which the Holy Ghost teacheth; comparing spiritual things with spiritual. 1 CORINTHIANS 2:13

Torrey faced the obvious question: if the Spirit chose the words, why does Paul sound like Paul and John like John? His answer was that the Creator of human speech is quite able to use each writer’s own vocabulary and individuality in revealing His truth. The words are fully human and fully God’s. That is still the best short answer to the question.

Above all, Torrey pointed to the attitude of Jesus. The Lord treated the Old Testament as the Word of God, down to its smallest parts. The scripture, He said, cannot be broken.

For verily I say unto you, Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled. MATTHEW 5:18

Difficulties are to be expected

Torrey did not pretend there were no hard places in the Bible. “We have no desire to conceal the fact that these difficulties exist,” he wrote in How to Succeed in the Christian Life. He had seen young Christians whose faith went into eclipse for months because of them, and he wanted to help.

His first point was that difficulties are exactly what we should expect. The Bible is a revelation of the infinite God to finite and sinful people. If someone handed him a book as simple as the multiplication table and said it was God’s full revelation, he would not believe it.

For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, saith the LORD. For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts. ISAIAH 55:8–9

Peter himself admitted that some things in Paul’s letters are hard to be understood.

As also in all his epistles, speaking in them of these things; in which are some things hard to be understood, which they that are unlearned and unstable wrest, as they do also the other scriptures, unto their own destruction. 2 PETER 3:16

His second point was that a difficulty does not disprove a doctrine. Every great scientific theory has faced objections that could not at first be answered, and has been rightly held because the positive evidence was strong. The fact that you cannot solve a difficulty does not prove it cannot be solved. Torrey liked to remind his readers of a beginner in algebra who, failing to solve a problem in half an hour, declared it insoluble.

How to handle them

His counsel on dealing with difficulties is some of the best practical advice he ever gave. Deal with them, he said, honestly, humbly, determinedly, fearlessly, patiently, scripturally and prayerfully.

Honestly: “If you cannot give a good honest explanation, do not attempt as yet to give any at all.” That sentence deserves to be better known. A forced answer does more harm than an honest I do not yet know.

Humbly: remember the limits of your own knowledge.

Determinedly: “The difficulties in the Bible are your heavenly Father’s challenge to you to set your brains to work.”

Fearlessly: you are not likely to find a difficulty that was not seen and faced centuries ago, and the Book still stands.

Patiently: lay a problem aside for a while, and come back to it.

Scripturally: let clear passages shed light on obscure ones, never the reverse.

And prayerfully. “It is wonderful how difficulties dissolve when one looks at them on his knees.”

Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law. PSALM 119:18

Where to read him with care

Torrey’s doctrine of Scripture is the historic doctrine of the church, and his practical counsel is sound. But the reader should be aware of the manner in which he argued.

He wrote in a hard-fought controversy, and it shows. He was prone to state the alternatives as starkly as possible: either the Bible is what it claims to be or it is an outrageous fraud. He could speak with contempt of critics, as though none of them had studied the Bible seriously. His confidence that almost every difficulty would yield to a little more study reflects the rationalist optimism of his age, which believed that evidence properly marshalled would settle every question.

A more patient reader today can hold Torrey’s conclusion firmly while admitting that some difficulties are genuinely hard, that honest scholars have wrestled with them for a lifetime, and that some may not be resolved this side of glory. That is not a weaker faith in Scripture. It is the humility Torrey himself recommended, and it rests on the same foundation: that the God who speaks in Scripture does not lie.

The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever, that we may do all the words of this law. DEUTERONOMY 29:29
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Ask yourself whether you treat the Bible as a final court of appeal, or as good advice to be taken when it suits you.

2. Write down one difficulty in the Bible that troubles you. Resolve to face it honestly, humbly and prayerfully rather than avoid it.

3. If someone asks you a question about the Bible that you cannot answer, practise saying honestly that you do not yet know, and offer to look into it together.

4. Spend time this week not on the difficulties of Scripture but on its glories. Read a chapter such as Isaiah 53 or John 17 slowly and with wonder.

5. Take one hard passage to God on your knees before you take it to a commentary.

A PRAYER
Lord God, You have spoken, and Your word is pure, like silver tried in a furnace. I thank You for the Scriptures.
Where I do not understand, give me honesty to admit it, humility to wait, and diligence to seek.
Keep me from pride in my questions and from fear of them. Let me come to hard places on my knees.
And let me not only defend Your Word but do it, for the glory of Jesus Christ, of whom it speaks. Amen.
