fields.title: What Think Ye of Christ?
fields.body_html:
Saying, What think ye of Christ? whose son is he? They say unto him, The Son of David. MATTHEW 22:42

Torrey was sure that everything turns on the person of Jesus Christ. “If a man really holds right views concerning the person of Jesus Christ,” he said in The Fundamental Doctrines of the Christian Faith, “he will sooner or later get right views on every other question.” And the reverse was just as true: go wrong about Christ, and you will sooner or later go wrong about everything else. So the question Jesus put to the Pharisees is the question to put to every person in every age. What think ye of Christ?

Old words, new meanings

Torrey noticed something in his own day that has not gone away. When he was a boy, he said, to believe in the divinity of Christ meant to believe that Jesus was actually God. By the time he preached these sermons, the phrase could mean almost anything — that Jesus was a great man in whom the divine shone more brightly than in others. The subtlest way to spread error, he observed, is to keep the old precious words and pour a new meaning into them. So he refused to ask merely whether Jesus was divine. He asked whether Jesus is God.

The case from Scripture

His method was his usual one: gather the texts and let them speak. He arranged them under heads.

First, divine names are given to Christ. He is called God outright.

In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. JOHN 1:1

Thomas, confronted by the risen Lord, did not correct himself.

And Thomas answered and said unto him, My Lord and my God. JOHN 20:28

And the letter to the Hebrews applies to the Son words spoken of God.

But unto the Son he saith, Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever: a sceptre of righteousness is the sceptre of thy kingdom. HEBREWS 1:8

Second, divine attributes are ascribed to Him: all power, eternity — before Abraham was, I am — and changelessness, for He is the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever. Third, divine offices belong to Him: upholding all things, forgiving sins, raising the dead, judging the world and giving eternal life. Fourth, passages the Old Testament says of Jehovah are applied in the New Testament to Jesus. Fifth, His name is coupled with the Father’s in ways that would be blasphemous if He were a creature. And sixth, He receives worship.

That all men should honour the Son, even as they honour the Father. He that honoureth not the Son honoureth not the Father which hath sent him. JOHN 5:23

The claims of Jesus

The part of Torrey’s sermon that most repays reading is his list of what he called incidental proofs — the things Jesus said about Himself in passing that no mere man could say.

Jesus invited all the weary of the world to come to Him for rest.

Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. MATTHEW 11:28

Anyone who makes a promise like that, Torrey said, must be God, or a lunatic, or an impostor.

Jesus asked for the same faith that is given to God.

Let not your heart be troubled: ye believe in God, believe also in me. JOHN 14:1

Torrey set this beside Jeremiah’s curse on the man who trusts in man, and concluded that Christ was either God or a deceiver. Jesus demanded a love greater than the love of father and mother. He said that He and the Father are one, and that whoever had seen Him had seen the Father.

Jesus saith unto him, Have I been so long time with you, and yet hast thou not known me, Philip? he that hath seen me hath seen the Father; and how sayest thou then, Shew us the Father? JOHN 14:9

A real man

Torrey was just as insistent on the other side. His next sermon was titled Jesus Christ a Real Man, and it deserves to be read beside the first. Jesus had a human mother and grew as a child grows. He was weary, hungry and thirsty. He was tempted. He prayed. And Torrey noted that Jesus did His mighty works not by drawing on His own deity but through the Holy Spirit who came upon Him at His baptism — a point that connects this doctrine directly to his teaching on the Spirit.

For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin. HEBREWS 4:15

And then Torrey put the matter as plainly as anyone has. “A merely divine Saviour could not be a Saviour for me. A merely human Saviour could not be a Saviour for me.” Only one who is both God and man can bear our sins, because He is God, and bear them for us, because He is man.

For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily. COLOSSIANS 2:9

What follows

Torrey’s conclusion was twofold. The first half was joy. The Saviour in whom we believe is God, and nothing is too hard for Him. He can save to the uttermost.

Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them. HEBREWS 7:25

The second half was warning. If Jesus is God, then to reject Him is not a small thing. Many people think themselves good because they have not stolen or murdered, Torrey said, while they are guilty of the gravest sin of all: rejecting a Saviour who is God. And denying a fact does not change it.

Where care is needed

Torrey’s doctrine here is the faith of the church, and his arguments are good. His manner is sometimes another matter. He ended the sermon by comparing those who deny Christ’s deity to a husband who slanders a faithful wife, and then left an insulting word unsaid for his hearers’ consciences to supply. It is the kind of rhetoric that may have stirred a congregation during the First World War, but it wins few doubters today and grieves the Spirit of the One it defends.

The reader who shares Torrey’s conviction does well to argue as clearly as he did and more gently. Many who question Christ’s deity have never seen Him as He is shown in the Gospels. They need to be shown Him, patiently, rather than shouted at.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Answer Christ’s question for yourself in writing: what do I think of Christ? Is He to me a great teacher, or my Lord and my God?

2. Read John 14:1–11 slowly, noting every claim Jesus makes about Himself.

3. Thank God today both that your Saviour is God, for whom nothing is too hard, and that He is a man who knows your weakness from the inside.

4. Bring one temptation you face this week to the Christ who was tempted in all points, and ask for His help.

5. Think of someone who doubts that Jesus is God. Pray for them, and look for a gentle way to point them to the Christ of the Gospels.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus Christ, You are the Word who was with God and was God, and You became flesh and dwelt among us. I worship You.
I thank You that nothing is too hard for You, and that You are able to save me to the uttermost.
I thank You that You were weary and tempted as I am, and that You understand me.
Let me confess You with Thomas as my Lord and my God, and honour You as I honour the Father. Amen.

fields.title: The Atonement
fields.body_html:
But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all. ISAIAH 53:5–6

Torrey said of the atonement exactly what he had said of the person of Christ: if a man holds right views about it he will sooner or later get right on everything else, and if he goes wrong here he is likely to go wrong everywhere. His sermon on the subject in The Fundamental Doctrines of the Christian Faith is long, crowded with texts, and fiercely polemical. Beneath the polemics is a clear and moving account of why Christ died.

One question, asked five times

The sermon contains a story that shows Torrey at his most characteristic. Teaching a Bible class in Minneapolis, he remarked in passing that Christian Science denied the atonement through the blood of Christ. A courteous woman came to him afterwards to say that he misunderstood; Christian Science did teach the atonement. So he asked her a single question: did she believe that Jesus Christ bore her sins in His own body on the cross? She answered that Christian Science was a beautiful system. He asked again. She said it had done her much good. He asked again, and again, and she spoke of Christ’s beautiful life and of lovely people and of following Jesus. At last she said, that is a doctrinal question.

Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness: by whose stripes ye were healed. 1 PETER 2:24

Torrey’s point was not to score off a lady. It was that many people use the word atonement while denying what it means, and the only way to find out is to ask the plain question. He thought the same was true in many pulpits of his day. The word had been kept and the substance emptied out.

The centre of the Bible

Torrey began by showing how central the death of Christ is. It is mentioned directly well over a hundred times in the New Testament, and foreshadowed throughout the Old. Christ took flesh and blood in order that He might die.

Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same; that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil. HEBREWS 2:14

When Moses and Elijah appeared with Him on the mount of transfiguration, what they spoke of was His decease which He should accomplish at Jerusalem. And the song of heaven is a song about His death.

And they sung a new song, saying, Thou art worthy to take the book, and to open the seals thereof: for thou wast slain, and hast redeemed us to God by thy blood out of every kindred, and tongue, and people, and nation. REVELATION 5:9

A gospel that is embarrassed by the cross, Torrey argued, is not the gospel of the Bible. It is not the song of heaven.

Why He died

Torrey then set out, in the orderly way he loved, what Scripture says about the purpose of Christ’s death.

He died as a substitute: the righteous for the unrighteous, bearing what we deserved.

For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him. 2 CORINTHIANS 5:21

He died as a ransom, the price paid to set others free. Jesus said so Himself.

Even as the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many. MATTHEW 20:28

He died as a sin offering, on the ground of which alone forgiveness is offered. He died as a propitiation, turning away God’s holy wrath against sin. He died to redeem us from the curse of the law by being made a curse for us. And He died as our Passover, so that God’s judgement passes over those who shelter under His blood.

Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree. GALATIANS 3:13

What His death has won

The last part of the sermon lists the results of the atonement, and it is here that Torrey’s tone softens into wonder. Through Christ’s death a propitiation is provided for the whole world, so that the gospel can be offered to every person without exception.

And he is the propitiation for our sins: and not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world. 1 JOHN 2:2

Believers have forgiveness of all their sins. More than that, they are justified — and Torrey was careful to explain that justification is more than forgiveness. Forgiveness puts away our sins; justification reckons us righteous. Because of the blood of Christ, the believer may enter with boldness into the very presence of God.

Having therefore, brethren, boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus, By a new and living way, which he hath consecrated for us, through the veil, that is to say, his flesh. HEBREWS 10:19–20

Believers will live with Christ forever and receive an eternal inheritance. And Torrey saw the atonement reaching even to the created order, reconciling all things in heaven and earth. He ended with words that are worth carrying away: the blood of Christ “has a power and efficiency, the fullness of which only eternity will disclose.”

Where care is needed

The substance of Torrey’s teaching here is the teaching of the Reformation and of historic evangelical faith, and it should be held firmly. Its manner is another matter.

He named Mary Baker Eddy and the Unitarians repeatedly, and said the devil had inspired their teaching. He listed denomination after denomination whose pulpits he thought compromised. He was fighting a real battle, and he was right that the substitutionary death of Christ was being quietly abandoned in many places. But the reader who shares his convictions need not share his combative tone, and should be slow to assume the worst of every person who is confused about the cross. The woman in the Minneapolis class was not a teacher of error; she was someone who had never been shown what Christ had done for her.

The better use of Torrey’s sermon is the use he himself would have wanted: not to win arguments but to see, and help others see, that Christ bore our sins.

For I delivered unto you first of all that which I also received, how that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures. 1 CORINTHIANS 15:3
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Ask yourself Torrey’s plain question and answer it aloud: do I believe that Jesus Christ bore my sins in His own body on the cross?

2. Read Isaiah 53 slowly, and underline every phrase that speaks of Christ bearing what we deserved.

3. Choose one of the pictures of the atonement — substitute, ransom, propitiation, curse-bearer, Passover — and meditate on it for a week.

4. Next time you pray, come boldly into God’s presence, consciously resting on the blood of Christ and not on your own performance.

5. If you know someone who uses Christian words without their meaning, pray for an opportunity to ask them, gently, what they believe Christ did on the cross.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You were wounded for my transgressions and bruised for my iniquities. You bore my sins in Your own body on the tree.
You were made sin for me, who knew no sin, that I might be made the righteousness of God in You. I cannot understand it, but I believe it, and I thank You.
Let me never be ashamed of Your cross, nor empty it of its meaning, nor treat it as a doctrine only.
Teach me to sing even now the song of heaven: Thou art worthy, for Thou wast slain. Amen.

fields.title: Justified and Born Again
fields.body_html:
But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness. ROMANS 4:5

Two sermons in The Fundamental Doctrines of the Christian Faith belong together. One is on justification by faith, which Torrey called the distinctive doctrine of Protestantism. The other is on the new birth. The first is about what God does for us: He declares us righteous. The second is about what God does in us: He gives us a new nature. Torrey held both with equal firmness and was careful never to confuse them.

What justification is

Torrey began, as always, by defining his terms. There are two different ideas of what it means to justify. One is to make righteous. The other is to reckon, declare or show to be righteous. Everything depends on which is meant, and Torrey argued that Scripture means the second. Justification is God’s verdict, not a process in our character. The ungodly are justified, not the reformed.

And by him all that believe are justified from all things, from which ye could not be justified by the law of Moses. ACTS 13:39

How we are justified

Torrey then answered the question how, piece by piece. Not by the works of the law, because no one keeps the law. Freely, by God’s grace, as a gift and not a wage.

Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. ROMANS 3:24

On the ground of Christ’s shed blood, which satisfies the justice of God. And on the condition of faith, so that God is at once just and the justifier of the one who believes.

To declare, I say, at this time his righteousness: that he might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus. ROMANS 3:26

The vilest woman in Chicago

Torrey told a story that he clearly loved, and it appears in both The Fundamental Doctrines and his sermon The Most Important Question. Preaching one Sunday in the Chicago Avenue Church on there is therefore now no condemnation, he said that if the vilest woman in Chicago came into the church that morning and put her trust in Jesus Christ, “every sin she ever committed would be blotted out and her record would be as white in God’s sight as that of the purest woman in the room.”

Unknown to him, a member of his congregation had gone that very morning into one of the lowest houses in the city and begged a woman living there to come and hear him. The woman had refused at first, and then agreed to follow a few steps behind. She slipped into the back row just as he spoke those words. She believed them, and at the end of the service she came to the front in tears to thank him.

Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. ROMANS 5:1

Torrey added that justification is more than a clean record. The perfect righteousness of Christ is put to the believer’s account, so that he is as near and dear to God as Christ Himself. Wondrous doctrine, he said. Glorious doctrine. He was right.

Faith that works

Torrey was careful to guard the doctrine from misuse. James says a man is justified by works and not by faith only, and some see a contradiction with Paul. Torrey saw none. Paul, he said, speaks against legalism: we are justified on the single condition of real faith. James speaks against antinomianism: the faith that justifies is real faith, and real faith shows itself in action. He quoted with approval a saying he attributed to someone else — that we are justified by faith without works, but not by a faith that is without works.

Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone. JAMES 2:17

Born again

The new birth, Torrey said, is the impartation of a new nature — God’s own nature.

Whereby are given unto us exceeding great and precious promises: that by these ye might be partakers of the divine nature, having escaped the corruption that is in the world through lust. 2 PETER 1:4

We are all born with a corrupted nature, blind to the things of God. In the new birth God does not simply improve that nature. He gives a new one. And Torrey traced the results through Scripture: the body becomes a temple of the Holy Spirit; the law of the Spirit sets the believer free from the law of sin; the mind is renewed; the believer believes that Jesus is the Christ, overcomes the world, does not go on in sin, and loves the brethren.

Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new. 2 CORINTHIANS 5:17

The necessity he took straight from the lips of Jesus.

Jesus answered and said unto him, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God. JOHN 3:3

How it happens

Torrey held together two truths that are often pulled apart. Regeneration is God’s work alone; we are saved by the washing of regeneration and renewing of the Holy Ghost. But that does not mean we must wait passively for God to act. We are born again by the Word of God, received by faith.

Being born again, not of corruptible seed, but of incorruptible, by the word of God, which liveth and abideth for ever. 1 PETER 1:23

He summed it up in a picture: “In the New Birth the Word of God is the seed; the human heart is the soil; the preacher of the Word is the sower.” The Spirit opens the heart, the hearer believes, the Spirit quickens the seed, and a new life springs up.

But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name: Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God. JOHN 1:12–13

A word of balance

Torrey’s teaching here is sound, and his distinction between justification and regeneration is one many Christians would do well to learn. The only caution concerns his list of the marks of the new birth. Read quickly, it can suggest that a true Christian never struggles, never doubts and never falls. Torrey did not mean that, and elsewhere he said plainly that believers still have the flesh. The marks describe the direction of a life, not a flawless record. A struggling believer should look first to the promise of justification — all that believe are justified from all things — and only then to the evidence of new life, which may be small but is real.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Put in your own words the difference between being justified and being born again.

2. Ask whether you are trusting in any way to your own improvement for acceptance with God. Rest instead on Christ’s blood and righteousness alone.

3. Thank God specifically that as a believer you are justified from all things, including the sin that troubles you most.

4. Look for one practical way this week in which your faith can show itself in works.

5. Pray for someone you think of as beyond reach, remembering the woman who slipped into the back row of the Chicago Avenue Church.

A PRAYER
Father, I come to You as one of the ungodly, with nothing to offer but faith in Your Son. Thank You that You justify the ungodly.
Thank You that every sin I have committed is blotted out, and that the righteousness of Christ is put to my account.
Thank You too for the new birth, by Your Word and Spirit. Let the new life You have given show itself in love, in obedience and in victory over the world.
And give me the joy of sowing Your Word in other hearts, that they too may be born again. Amen.

fields.title: Because God Says So
fields.body_html:
These things have I written unto you that believe on the name of the Son of God; that ye may know that ye have eternal life, and that ye may believe on the name of the Son of God. 1 JOHN 5:13

If there is one phrase that sums up Torrey, it is because God says so. Nowhere is it more at home than in his teaching on assurance. He believed that a Christian may know — not hope, not suppose, but know — that his sins are forgiven and that he has eternal life. And he believed that the ground of that knowledge is not feeling but the plain testimony of God in His Word.

Can a believer know

Torrey knew the objection well: no one can know he is saved until he stands before God at the judgement. He answered it with 1 John 5:13. John wrote his letter for the express purpose that believers might know that they have eternal life. To deny that they can, Torrey said in How to Succeed in the Christian Life, is to say the letter was written in vain.

Feelings and facts

How, then, does anyone know? Torrey’s answer was always the same: on the best ground of knowledge there is, the testimony of God Himself.

He that believeth on the Son hath everlasting life: and he that believeth not the Son shall not see life; but the wrath of God abideth on him. JOHN 3:36

Anyone can know whether he believes on the Son. If he does, he has God’s written word that he has everlasting life. He may feel forgiven or he may not. “It is not a question of what we feel but of what God says,” Torrey wrote. God’s Word is always to be believed. Our feelings are often to be doubted.

He illustrated it with a pardon. Suppose you were in prison and your friends obtained a pardon for you. The document is handed to you, and the news is so sudden that you are dazed; you do not feel pardoned. Someone asks, Are you pardoned? You say yes. Do you feel pardoned? No, not yet. Then how do you know? You hold up the document: This says so. In time, after reading it over and over, you will feel it too. The Bible, Torrey said, is God’s document declaring that everyone who believes in Jesus is justified.

God’s word as good as mine

In How to Bring Men to Christ he told a story that makes the point better than any argument. A young man had come forward in deep distress two nights running. He professed to have accepted Christ but had no assurance. Torrey showed him John 3:36 and the young man still saw nothing. As he turned to leave, he asked Torrey to pray for him. Torrey said he would. Then he called him back down the aisle and asked: Do you believe I will pray for you? The young man was astonished — of course. Why? Because you said so. “Isn’t God’s word as good as mine?” Torrey asked. The young man saw it at once. He had been willing to take a man’s word and not God’s. He received assurance on the spot.

He that believeth on the Son of God hath the witness in himself: he that believeth not God hath made him a liar; because he believeth not the record that God gave of his Son. And this is the record, that God hath given to us eternal life, and this life is in his Son. 1 JOHN 5:10–11

Torrey drew the uncomfortable conclusion John draws. For a believer to doubt that he has eternal life is, in effect, to make God a liar. It is not humility. It is unbelief dressed as humility.

Dealing with the doubting

In How to Bring Men to Christ Torrey gave practical counsel for helping those who lack assurance. He divided them into two groups. Some lack it through ignorance: they have simply never been told that the Bible says believers may know. For them he used verses such as John 1:12, John 3:36, John 5:24 and Acts 13:39, and he would take the inquirer through a verse with questions until the inquirer said for himself what God said.

Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that heareth my word, and believeth on him that sent me, hath everlasting life, and shall not come into condemnation; but is passed from death unto life. JOHN 5:24

Others lack assurance because of sin, and for them the remedy is not more verses but confession and a return to obedience. Torrey was careful to distinguish the two. Assurance cannot be talked into someone who is living in known disobedience, and should not be.

Looking unto Jesus

Torrey connected assurance to a habit he commended in How to Succeed in the Christian Life: keep looking at Jesus. Satan, he said, will try again and again to discourage believers by bringing up their sins. If he can get us brooding over them, he will soon have us discouraged, and discouragement means failure. The answer is to look where God looks — at the death of Christ in our place.

For the which cause I also suffer these things: nevertheless I am not ashamed: for I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him against that day. 2 TIMOTHY 1:12

“It is an act of base ingratitude to God,” he wrote, “to brood over sins that He in His infinite love has cancelled.” That sentence has freed many a tender conscience.

Where care is needed

Torrey’s method has helped thousands of genuinely anxious believers, and it rests on firm ground. God’s Word is the foundation of assurance.

But there is a danger, and Torrey knew it, because he wrote a whole chapter in the same book on those who entertain false hopes. Leading someone to say the words I have everlasting life because God says so is powerful when that person truly believes. It can also produce false assurance in someone who has given only a verbal assent, especially when an eager worker presses for the words. Scripture itself tells us to examine ourselves.

Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves. Know ye not your own selves, how that Jesus Christ is in you, except ye be reprobates? 2 CORINTHIANS 13:5

The same letter John wrote so that believers might know gives marks of new life: obedience, love for the brethren, belief that Jesus is the Christ. These do not replace the promise; they confirm it. The best counsel is Torrey’s, held with a little more care than he sometimes showed: rest your assurance on what God says about Christ, and let the fruit of new life, over time, confirm that your faith is real.

We know that we have passed from death unto life, because we love the brethren. He that loveth not his brother abideth in death. 1 JOHN 3:14
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Answer honestly: do you know that you have eternal life? On what ground — your feelings, your record, or what God says?

2. Read John 3:36 and 1 John 5:10–13 aloud. Ask yourself Torrey’s questions: who has everlasting life? do I believe on the Son? what, then, do I have?

3. If you are troubled by past sin that you have already confessed, stop brooding over it. Thank God that it is cancelled.

4. If you lack assurance because of known disobedience, deal with that first. Confess it and return.

5. Think of someone who doubts their salvation. Ask God for an opportunity to show them what He says.

A PRAYER
Faithful God, You have written these things so that I may know that I have eternal life. Forgive me for trusting my feelings more than Your Word.
I believe on Your Son. You say that whoever believes on the Son has everlasting life. I take You at Your word.
When Satan brings up my sins, turn my eyes to the cross, where they were borne and settled.
And let the life You have given show itself in obedience and love, to Your glory. Amen.

fields.title: How to Succeed in the Christian Life
fields.body_html:
Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us, Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith. HEBREWS 12:1–2

Torrey wrote How to Succeed in the Christian Life for young converts, many of them brought to Christ in his great missions. It is a plain handbook, with chapters on Bible study, prayer, working for Christ and the rest, and some of its counsel has already appeared in this volume. This chapter gathers the rest of it: how to begin, how to confess Christ, how to choose companions and recreations, how to meet persecution, and how to be guided. The title may sound like a self-help manual. The content is nothing of the kind. Success, for Torrey, meant going on with Christ.

Beginning right

“There is nothing more important in the Christian life than beginning right,” Torrey wrote. And he added a comfort: anyone who has begun wrong can begin again, and begin right.

The right beginning is receiving Jesus Christ. To receive Him means to take Him to be to yourself all that God offers Him to be. Torrey named three things. God offers Jesus as our sin-bearer, so that we are forgiven not because of our good works but solely because of His death. He offers Him as our deliverer from the power of sin, a living Saviour able to keep us day by day. And He offers Him as our Lord and Master, to whom we surrender the control of our lives.

But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name. JOHN 1:12

Open confession

The next step is to confess Christ openly.

Whosoever therefore shall confess me before men, him will I confess also before my Father which is in heaven. MATTHEW 10:32

Many try to be disciples without letting the world know. No one has succeeded. “To be a secret disciple means to be no disciple at all,” Torrey wrote. And confession is not something done once, at baptism or at the front of a meeting. It is to be constant. In his sermon Heroes and Cowards he preached on the fear of man that is a snare, the snare that catches the young man who takes his first drink because the table laughs at him, and the one that keeps many from confessing Christ.

The fear of man bringeth a snare: but whoso putteth his trust in the LORD shall be safe. PROVERBS 29:25

The church and companions

Torrey had no patience with the idea that a Christian can do without the church. No Christian, young or old, can succeed without the fellowship of other believers. The church is made of imperfect people and is therefore an imperfect institution, but it is of divine origin, God loves it, and every believer should take his place in it. Those who stand aloof from every church in the hope of a broader fellowship with all believers, he observed, deceive themselves; they miss the help that comes from belonging to one local congregation.

The chapter on amusements shows Torrey at his most time-bound, and also at his most sensible. He did not attempt a list of forbidden pastimes; he said it was neither possible nor necessary. Torrey warned new Christians plainly that persecution would come. It may not be prison or death, but the world still hates God, and it will find a way to make the loyal follower of Christ pay. Torrey counted keeping one’s eyes on Christ as one of the simplest and mightiest secrets of the Christian life. We look to the crucified Christ for pardon and to the risen Christ for daily victory. Finally, Torrey spoke to the many earnest Christians tormented by the question of God’s will. Give me faithful friends, a place among Your people, and recreations I can enjoy in Your presence.

fields.title: How to Bring Men to Christ
fields.body_html:
The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life; and he that winneth souls is wise. PROVERBS 11:30

Torrey preached to vast crowds, but he believed that the most important evangelism happens one person at a time. His handbook How to Bring Men to Christ, written in his Chicago years, is a manual for what was then called personal work: sitting down with one individual, Bible open, and helping him to Christ. He wrote it for ordinary Christians, not for ministers, because he believed that every believer is called to this work. In How to Succeed in the Christian Life he put it bluntly: Jesus said, Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men, and anyone who is not fishing is not following.

And he saith unto them, Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men. MATTHEW 4:19

The conditions of success

The book opens with five conditions which, Torrey said, are few and simple and within anyone’s reach.

The worker must himself be thoroughly converted, turned from sin and worldliness with his whole heart, with Christ as Lord of his thoughts and actions.

He must have a love for souls. Without it, his words will be mechanical. How is it to be had? Torrey’s answer is practical. Confess the lack and ask God for it. Keep close company with Christ, who loved the lost. And think. “Feelings are the outcome of thoughts,” he wrote; dwell long enough on the peril of a person without Christ and on what Christ paid to save him, and longing for his salvation will follow.

That I have great heaviness and continual sorrow in my heart. For I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh. ROMANS 9:2–3

He must have a working knowledge of the Bible, for the Word is the sword of the Spirit. He must know how to show a person his need of a Saviour, show him Christ, show him how to receive Christ, and meet his difficulties.

He must pray much: that God will lead him to the right person, show him what to say, give power to the words, and carry on the work afterwards. Torrey thought this the thing the average worker in a hurried age most needed to hear. By praying more, he wrote, we will not work any less, and we will accomplish vastly more.

Then the Spirit said unto Philip, Go near, and join thyself to this chariot. ACTS 8:29

And he must be endued with the power of the Holy Spirit, the subject to which the book’s last chapter returns.

How to begin

Torrey knew that the hardest moment is the first one. In a meeting it is easy to ask someone whether he is a Christian. With a stranger it takes more care, though often, he said, a courteous and direct question is best. He told of passing a man on a crowded Chicago street, feeling an impulse to speak to him, asking God whether it was from Him, and then turning back, laying a hand on the man’s shoulder and asking, “My friend, are you a Christian?” The man said it was a strange question. Torrey replied that he did not ask it of every stranger, but God had put it into his heart. The man, it turned out, was an Amherst graduate ruined by drink, whose cousin, a minister, had been pressing the same question on him. He later accepted Christ.

Every kind of person

The bulk of the book is a series of chapters on different kinds of people: the indifferent, the anxious who do not know how to be saved, those with difficulties, those with false hopes, those who lack assurance, backsliders, sceptics, the complaining, those who want to put off a decision, and the wilful. For each, Torrey supplied Scripture passages and advice on how to use them.

This part of the book can look mechanical today, like a filing system of texts. But it rests on a sound conviction: that people differ, that the Word of God has something fitted to each, and that a worker who has taken the trouble to know his Bible will be ready. His counsel for honest sceptics, for example, includes John 7:17: let a man set out to do God’s will, and he will come to know whether the teaching is of God.

If any man will do his will, he shall know of the doctrine, whether it be of God, or whether I speak of myself. JOHN 7:17

Hints worth keeping

The chapter of hints near the end is full of wisdom. Deal with people one at a time and, where possible, alone, for few will open their hearts in company. Have the person read the verse himself, so that truth enters through the eye as well as the ear. Often use a single passage and drive it home. Keep to the main point — Christ — and do not be drawn into side issues such as denominations or theories of future punishment until the first question is settled.

Be courteous. “It is quite possible to be at once perfectly frank and perfectly courteous,” Torrey wrote; the gentler the manner, the deeper the words go. Be in earnest, and let the passages you use first master you. “A few passages that have mastered us are better than many passages that we have mastered from some text book.” Never lose your temper. And he added, with real humility for the author of a handbook, that genuine earnestness will go further than any skill learned in a training class or from a book such as his.

Therefore watch, and remember, that by the space of three years I ceased not to warn every one night and day with tears. ACTS 20:31

Weighing it

How to Bring Men to Christ still repays reading. Its insistence that every Christian can and should speak of Christ is right, and its practical advice is better than much that has been written since.

Two cautions. The first is that Torrey’s confidence can make evangelism sound like a technique with a guaranteed outcome, and his sharp remark in How to Succeed in the Christian Life that anyone not fishing is not following could make a shy believer despair. Most Christians will not stop strangers in the street. All can pray, love, speak of Christ to those God puts in their path, and be ready to give a reason for the hope that is in them.

But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear. 1 PETER 3:15

The second is that pressing a person to a decision, which Torrey did with great skill, can produce professions that are not real. His own chapter on false hopes shows he knew it. The worker’s job is to point to Christ faithfully and leave the new birth to the Spirit.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Ask God today to give you a genuine love for those without Christ, and spend a few minutes thinking of one person’s need and Christ’s cost.

2. Choose three passages of Scripture that show someone how to be saved, and let them master you before you use them.

3. Pray each morning this week that God will lead you to one person, and show you what to say.

4. When a conversation turns to faith, keep it to the main point — Christ — and leave side issues for later.

5. Practise being at once perfectly frank and perfectly courteous in speaking of Christ.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You came to seek and to save that which was lost, and You call me to follow You as a fisher of men.
Give me love for souls, a working knowledge of Your Word, and the power of Your Spirit.
Lead me to the people You have prepared, and give me words that are frank and gentle, earnest and kind.
And when I have spoken, carry on the work that I cannot finish, for Your glory. Amen.

fields.title: The Uplifted Christ
fields.body_html:
And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me. JOHN 12:32

Torrey’s books on doctrine and devotion were written for Christians. His sermons were preached, most of them, to people who were not. The fourteen in the Ochorus library come largely from his great missions, several of them preached in London, and they show the evangelist at work. They are plain, direct, often stern, and always aimed at a decision. This chapter looks at what he preached when he stood before the crowds.

What drew them

In The Great Attraction: The Uplifted Christ, Torrey told of a church advertisement he had seen offering a film, a popular pianist and an opera singer as attractions for a Sunday evening service. It startled him that anyone should think the gospel needed propping up. “There is nothing else that draws like the uplifted Christ,” he said.

He spoke from experience. In London he had seen the Royal Albert Hall filled afternoon and evening for two months. A London reporter had told him no one had ever tried to hold two weeks of meetings there, and that not even Gladstone could have filled it for two weeks. The preacher, Torrey said of himself, was no remarkable orator, and the newspapers kept saying so. What filled the hall was Christ, preached and sung in the power of the Spirit, in answer to the prayers of many thousands of people around the world.

God is love

The sermon The Greatest Sentence That Was Ever Written opened one of his missions. Its text is three short words.

He that loveth not knoweth not God; for God is love. 1 JOHN 4:8

This, said Torrey, sums up the whole Bible. “The Bible is simply God’s love story, the story of the love of a holy God to a sinful world.” He told how Moody had the text written in gas jets above the pulpit of the Chicago church, and of a half-drunk man who pushed open the door on a stormy night, saw the words blazing, and walked away muttering that God could not love a wretch like him — and then came back, and was found at the end of the meeting weeping like a child.

But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. ROMANS 5:8

It is worth remembering this sermon when reading Torrey’s sterner ones. His warnings were the warnings of a man who believed that God is love.

What shall I do with Jesus

Many of his sermons turn on a single question. The Most Important Question takes Pilate’s words.

Pilate saith unto them, What shall I do then with Jesus which is called Christ? They all say unto him, Let him be crucified. MATTHEW 27:22

It is the most important question anyone ever asked or answered, Torrey said, because everything worth having depends on the answer — acceptance with God, peace, power, eternal life. And no one can avoid answering it. To do nothing with Christ is itself an answer.

The Way of Salvation Made Plain takes the Philippian jailer’s question and gives Paul’s answer without embellishment.

And brought them out, and said, Sirs, what must I do to be saved? And they said, Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved, and thy house. ACTS 16:30–31

Excuses and refuges

Torrey was relentless in stripping away the reasons people give for not coming to Christ. In Excuses, from the parable of the great supper, he pointed out that the excuses in Jesus’ story are absurd, and that this is the point. Who buys a field without seeing it, or oxen without trying them? No one would refuse an invitation to a royal banquet. Yet when God spreads His table, people hunt for reasons not to come.

And they all with one consent began to make excuse. The first said unto him, I have bought a piece of ground, and I must needs go and see it: I pray thee have me excused. LUKE 14:18

In Refuges of Lies he observed that the trouble with most people is not that they have no refuge but that they have a false one — morality, indifference, a vague trust in God’s kindness. He offered tests of a true refuge: does it satisfy the highest demands of your own conscience? Is it making you a better person? And he warned that the hail shall sweep away the refuge of lies.

Judgment also will I lay to the line, and righteousness to the plummet: and the hail shall sweep away the refuge of lies, and the waters shall overflow the hiding place. ISAIAH 28:17

And in Every Man’s Need of a Refuge he found the true refuge foretold in Isaiah: a man who would be a hiding place from the wind, a covert from the tempest, the shadow of a great rock in a weary land.

Today

The note on which nearly every one of these sermons ends is urgency. The Day of Golden Opportunity takes its text from the Holy Spirit’s word, To day.

Wherefore (as the Holy Ghost saith, To day if ye will hear his voice, Harden not your hearts. HEBREWS 3:7–8

Torrey told of a man who came to his office ruined by drink, agreed that he must turn to Christ, and when asked whether he would do it now, hung his head and said, not now, tomorrow. “Tomorrow is the devil’s day and the fool’s day,” Torrey said. “Today is God’s day, and the wise man’s day.”

Weighing it

These sermons are not subtle, and they were not meant to be. They use the illustrations and assumptions of their day — the coronation of King Edward, the dangers of the ballroom, the young man ruined by his first glass of wine — and a modern reader may smile. Some of their appeals press hard on fear.

But they have two great virtues. They are about Christ, and they ask for an answer. A great deal of preaching since has been more thoughtful and less clear. Torrey would have said that the business of the evangelist is to lift up Christ plainly and ask people what they will do with Him. The Holy Spirit does the drawing.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Ask whether you, or your church, have been tempted to make the gospel attractive by adding things to it rather than by lifting up Christ.

2. Answer Pilate’s question for yourself today: what have I done with Jesus?

3. Examine your own refuge. Is your hope before God resting on anything other than Christ?

fields.title: The Resurrection and the Coming Again
fields.body_html:
Which also said, Ye men of Galilee, why stand ye gazing up into heaven? this same Jesus, which is taken up from you into heaven, shall so come in like manner as ye have seen him go into heaven. ACTS 1:11

Torrey preached his sermon on the resurrection on an Easter Sunday at the Church of the Open Door, and it is printed in The Fundamental Doctrines of the Christian Faith. Its subject is not only the resurrection of Christ but the resurrection of our bodies, and it leads straight to the hope that shaped much of his preaching: the personal return of the Lord Jesus. He wrote a separate book on that return, which is not in the Ochorus library, but the theme runs through the sermons that are.

A risen body

Torrey began by noting a strange fact. Many people who called themselves orthodox Christians, he said, did not believe in the resurrection of the body at all. They believed in the immortality of the soul. That, he insisted, is not the Christian hope.

His argument was simple and careful. What was raised on the third day? Not the soul of Jesus, which did not die. Paul says that He died, that He was buried, and that He was raised — and what was buried was His body.

For I delivered unto you first of all that which I also received, how that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures. 1 CORINTHIANS 15:3–4

And when the risen Christ appeared to His disciples, He insisted that they handle Him.

Behold my hands and my feet, that it is I myself: handle me, and see; for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have. LUKE 24:39

What our bodies will be

Torrey took great care over the character of the resurrection body, and this part of the sermon is full of wonder. Drawing on 1 Corinthians 15 and other passages, he taught that it will not be exactly the body that was buried, any more than the plant is the seed, yet it will be continuous with it. It will be like Christ’s glorious body. It will be incorruptible, glorious, powerful and heavenly.

So also is the resurrection of the dead. It is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption: It is sown in dishonour; it is raised in glory: it is sown in weakness; it is raised in power. 1 CORINTHIANS 15:42–43

He dwelt especially on the word power. All our weariness and weakness, he said, will then be at an end. For a man who worked as hard as Torrey did, one can hear what that meant to him. And he saw the resurrection of the body as the completion of our adoption — the moment when the sons of God are fully revealed.

And not only they, but ourselves also, which have the firstfruits of the Spirit, even we ourselves groan within ourselves, waiting for the adoption, to wit, the redemption of our body. ROMANS 8:23

Between death and resurrection

Torrey asked what happens to believers who die before the Lord returns. His answer from 2 Corinthians 5 and Philippians 1 was that their spirits are unclothed — without their earthly body and not yet clothed with the resurrection body — but at home with the Lord in conscious blessedness. That state is far better than this life, though not so perfect as what will follow.

For I am in a strait betwixt two, having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better. PHILIPPIANS 1:23

It will be at the return of the Lord, he said, that we receive our full redemption.

Waiting for Him

That brought Torrey to the hope of Christ’s coming. The believer looks for the Saviour from heaven, who will change the body of our humiliation into the likeness of His own glorious body.

For our conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ: Who shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body, according to the working whereby he is able even to subdue all things unto himself. PHILIPPIANS 3:20–21

He gave several reasons for longing for that day. One was personal: the present body, useful as it is, is often a hindrance, subject to pain and frailty and temptation. Another was public. Torrey believed that the great problems of national and international life, of society and politics, would be solved when Christ came, and would never be solved until He came. The sermons in that volume were preached during the First World War, and one can feel the weight of the times on them.

For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first: Then we which are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air: and so shall we ever be with the Lord. 1 THESSALONIANS 4:16–17

Where care is needed

On the resurrection of Christ and of our bodies, Torrey stood squarely with the creeds, and he is a good guide. His warning that many Christians have quietly exchanged the resurrection for a vague immortality of the soul is still needed.

On the return of Christ, he held the premillennial view common among the evangelists and Bible teachers of his circle: that Christ will come before a literal thousand-year reign. Many faithful Christians have held other views, and the details of the order of events are matters on which Scripture has left room for disagreement. What all Christians confess is that He will come again, personally and visibly, to judge the living and the dead.

It is also worth guarding against one misuse of his hope. To say that the world’s problems will never be solved until Christ comes can make Christians indifferent to present injustice. Torrey did not mean that, and his own life, spent working among the poor in Minneapolis and training workers for the slums of Chicago, shows it. The hope of Christ’s return is meant to purify us and to spur us, not to excuse us.

Beloved, now are we the sons of God, and it doth not yet appear what we shall be: but we know that, when he shall appear, we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is. And every man that hath this hope in him purifieth himself, even as he is pure. 1 JOHN 3:2–3

And no one knows the day or the hour. The right posture is not calculation but readiness.

But of that day and hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels of heaven, but my Father only. MATTHEW 24:36
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Ask whether your hope for the future is the resurrection of the body or merely the survival of the soul. Read 1 Corinthians 15 this week.

2. If you are weary or in pain, meditate on the promise that the body sown in weakness will be raised in power.

3. If you have lost a believing friend, give thanks that they are at home with the Lord, and that there is a better day still to come.

4. Ask how the hope of Christ’s return is purifying you. Name one thing you would put right if you knew He was coming this week.

5. Resist the temptation to despair of the world or to ignore its needs. Pray for Christ’s coming, and do good while you wait.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You died, You were buried, and You rose again the third day. You are the firstfruits of them that sleep, and I believe that I too shall be raised.
Thank You that my weakness will be raised in power and my dishonour in glory, and that I shall be like You, for I shall see You as You are.
Keep me ready for Your coming. Let this hope purify me, and let it make me faithful and fruitful while I wait.
Even so, come, Lord Jesus. Amen.

fields.title: Is Future Punishment Everlasting?
fields.body_html:
And these shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal. MATTHEW 25:46

This is the hardest chapter in the book, and it would be dishonest to leave it out. Torrey preached two Sunday-evening sermons on hell at the Church of the Open Door — Is There a Literal Hell? and Is Future Punishment Everlasting? — and they close The Fundamental Doctrines of the Christian Faith. His sermon Where Will You Spend Eternity? presses the same subject on the conscience of an unconverted hearer. He spoke of it more directly than almost any preacher would today. This chapter sets out what he taught, why he taught it, and where a reader needs care.

Why he preached it

Torrey did not preach hell because he enjoyed it. He began the first sermon by saying that God does not wish anyone to perish, but that God has made us with the power of choice, and some will choose darkness. He was sorry they would. He would be willing to die to save them, he said; the Lord Jesus did die to save them. Then he gave his reason for the sermon: “I am going to preach about hell to keep as many of you as possible from going there.”

Say unto them, As I live, saith the Lord GOD, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that the wicked turn from his way and live: turn ye, turn ye from your evil ways; for why will ye die, O house of Israel? EZEKIEL 33:11

That is the right place to begin. Whatever else is said about this doctrine, the God of the Bible takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, and the preacher who speaks of judgement without that note has misrepresented Him.

How to settle the question

Torrey refused two ways of settling the matter. We cannot decide it by counting heads, he said, because majorities in science, philosophy and theology have often been wrong. And we cannot decide it by reasoning about what a good God must do, because finite creatures cannot judge what an infinitely wise and holy God will do. All we know about the future is what God has told us. “One ounce of God’s revelation,” he said, “is worth more than a thousand tons of man’s speculation.”

So the question is only: what does the Bible teach?

What the Bible says

Torrey went first to the words of Jesus, who spoke of hell more than anyone else in Scripture.

And if thy hand offend thee, cut it off: it is better for thee to enter into life maimed, than having two hands to go into hell, into the fire that never shall be quenched: Where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched. MARK 9:43–44

He took Matthew 25:46 as decisive for the question of duration. The same word describes the punishment of the wicked and the life of the righteous. He examined it with some care, noting that of its many uses in the New Testament most are in the phrase eternal life, which no one supposes to end. If the one is endless, he argued, so is the other.

He turned also to Paul, who speaks of everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord, and to Revelation, where the smoke of torment ascends for ever and ever.

Who shall be punished with everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord, and from the glory of his power. 2 THESSALONIANS 1:9

Tried to escape it

The most striking passage in the sermon is a personal one. “Time and time again,” Torrey said, “I have come up to this awful doctrine and tried to find some way of escape from it.” He did not find one. When he determined to be honest with the Bible and with himself, he said, he went back to his work with a heavier burden for souls.

That admission matters. Torrey was not a cold man reciting a dogma. He was a man who did not want this doctrine to be true, looked hard for a way out, and believed Scripture did not give him one. Whatever the reader concludes, that is an honest way to come to it.

He drew a practical conclusion. Those who truly believe in the eternal loss of the impenitent, he said, work as they never worked before for the salvation of the lost. To weaken the doctrine is to weaken the zeal.

And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell. MATTHEW 10:28

Where care is needed

Here the reader must think carefully, and there are several things to say.

First, the substance of Torrey’s teaching is the historic teaching of most of the church through most of its history: that there is a real judgement, that it is final, and that those who reject Christ will be separated from God forever. Jesus Himself taught it with great seriousness. It should not be lightly set aside.

Second, Torrey’s imagery was more literal and more lurid than Scripture requires. He preached of the impenitent looking out after ten million years and seeing no end. Scripture uses the language of fire, darkness, the worm and exclusion from God’s presence, and faithful interpreters have differed on how literally to take each image. What is certain is the reality and the seriousness, not every detail of the picture.

Third, some who love Christ and hold Scripture as God’s Word have concluded that the wicked will finally be destroyed rather than endlessly tormented. Torrey spoke of such people harshly, and claimed that anyone who holds a looser view loses power with God. That is an overstatement. The question should be argued from Scripture, with charity.

Fourth, his tone. He compared hell to the war then raging in Europe and told his hearers that hell was far worse, and that it was the destiny of some of them unless they repented soon. It is hard to read. But the reader should remember that he was speaking to an evening congregation that included many who were not Christians, and that he believed with his whole heart that they were in danger. Silence, if he was right, would have been the cruellest thing he could do.

And finally, the right response to this doctrine is not a debate but tears. Jesus wept over Jerusalem.

And when he was come near, he beheld the city, and wept over it, Saying, If thou hadst known, even thou, at least in this thy day, the things which belong unto thy peace! but now they are hid from thine eyes. LUKE 19:41–42

Torrey ended by urging his hearers to accept Christ at once. That is still the point. The God who warns is the God who sent His Son not to condemn the world but to save it. The Judge of all the earth will do right. Our part is to flee to Christ ourselves and to plead with others while it is called today.

For God sent not his Son into the world to condemn the world; but that the world through him might be saved. JOHN 3:17
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Read what Jesus Himself says about judgement in Matthew 25:31–46 and Mark 9:42–48. Let His seriousness, not anyone else’s rhetoric, shape your view.

2. Ask honestly whether you have quietly set this doctrine aside because it is uncomfortable, or because Scripture requires it.

3. Name three people you know who do not know Christ, and begin praying for them by name daily.

4. If you speak of judgement to others, ask God to let you do it with tears and not with harshness.

5. Thank God that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.

A PRAYER
Holy and righteous God, You have no pleasure in the death of the wicked. You sent Your Son not to condemn the world but to save it.
I tremble at the words of Jesus about judgement. Keep me from explaining them away, and keep me from speaking them without love.
Thank You that in Christ I am safe, not by my goodness but by His blood.
Give me a burden for those who are lost, and courage and tenderness to plead with them while it is called today. Amen.

Who shall be punished with everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord, and from the glory of his power. 2 THESSALONIANS 1:9 Tried to escape it The most striking passage in the sermon is a personal one. “Time and time again,” Torrey said, “I have come up to this awful doctrine and tried to find some way of escape from it.” He did not find one. When he determined to be honest with the Bible and with himself, he said, he went back to his work with a heavier burden for souls. That admission matters. Torrey was not a cold man reciting a dogma. He was a man who did not want this doctrine to be true, looked hard for a way out, and believed Scripture did not give him one. Whatever the reader concludes, that is an honest way to come to it. He drew a practical conclusion. Those who truly believe in the eternal loss of the impenitent, he said, work as they never worked before for the salvation of the lost. To weaken the doctrine is to weaken the zeal. And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell. MATTHEW 10:28 Where care is needed Here the reader must think carefully, and there are several things to say. First, the substance of Torrey’s teaching is the historic teaching of most of the church through most of its history: that there is a real judgement, that it is final, and that those who reject Christ will be separated from God forever. Jesus Himself taught it with great seriousness. It should not be lightly set aside. Second, Torrey’s imagery was more literal and more lurid than Scripture requires. He preached of the impenitent looking out after ten million years and seeing no end. Scripture uses the language of fire, darkness, the worm and exclusion from God’s presence, and faithful interpreters have differed on how literally to take each image. What is certain is the reality and the seriousness, not every detail of the picture. Third, some who love Christ and hold Scripture as God’s Word have concluded that the wicked will finally be destroyed rather than endlessly tormented. Torrey spoke of such people harshly, and claimed that anyone who holds a looser view loses power with God. That is an overstatement. The question should be argued from Scripture, with charity. Fourth, his tone. He compared hell to the war then raging in Europe and told his hearers that hell was far worse, and that it was the destiny of some of them unless they repented soon. It is hard to read. But the reader should remember that he was speaking to an evening congregation that included many who were not Christians, and that he believed with his whole heart that they were in danger. Silence, if he was right, would have been the cruellest thing he could do. And finally, the right response to this doctrine is not a debate but tears. Jesus wept over Jerusalem. And when he was come near, he beheld the city, and wept over it, Saying, If thou hadst known, even thou, at least in this thy day, the things which belong unto thy peace! but now they are hid from thine eyes. LUKE 19:41–42 Torrey ended by urging his hearers to accept Christ at once. That is still the point. The God who warns is the God who sent His Son not to condemn the world but to save it. The Judge of all the earth will do right. Our part is to flee to Christ ourselves and to plead with others while it is called today. For God sent not his Son into the world to condemn the world; but that the world through him might be saved. JOHN 3:17 FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION 1. Read what Jesus Himself says about judgement in Matthew 25:31–46 and Mark 9:42–48. Let His seriousness, not anyone else’s rhetoric, shape your view. 2. Ask honestly whether you have quietly set this doctrine aside because it is uncomfortable, or because Scripture requires it. 3. Name three people you know who do not know Christ, and begin praying for them by name daily. 4. If you speak of judgement to others, ask God to let you do it with tears and not with harshness. 5. Thank God that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. A PRAYER Holy and righteous God, You have no pleasure in the death of the wicked. You sent Your Son not to condemn the world but to save it. I tremble at the words of Jesus about judgement. Keep me from explaining them away, and keep me from speaking them without love. Thank You that in Christ I am safe, not by my goodness but by His blood. Give me a burden for those who are lost, and courage and tenderness to plead with them while it is called today. Amen.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away. MATTHEW 24:35

Eighteen chapters can make it look as though R. A. Torrey taught a great many things. In one sense he did; few teachers have ranged so widely, from the personality of the Holy Spirit to the right hour for Bible study. But underneath it all was one conviction, and everything else is that conviction applied. God has spoken plainly, and He means exactly what He says.

Follow it through and the shape appears. The Spirit is a Person because Scripture ascribes to Him knowledge, will and love. The Father gives the Holy Spirit to them that ask Him because Jesus said so. Prayer according to God’s will is heard because John says so. The Bible is the Word of God because it claims to be and Christ treated it so. Jesus is God because He is called God and claimed what only God may claim. The believer is justified from all things, and may know he has eternal life, because God says so. Every Christian should speak to others of Christ because Christ called His followers fishers of men. And judgement is real because Jesus warned of it. One habit of mind, applied with remarkable consistency for fifty years.

The danger of this book

A reader who has come this far may be in some danger, and Torrey’s own story shows what it is. A teacher so confident, so practical, so full of steps and rules and conditions, can leave his readers with a new law. Seven steps to the baptism with the Spirit. Three times of prayer a day. Fifteen minutes of Bible study at least. A list of ways power is lost. A soul to be spoken to every day. Each of these is good counsel. Together, taken in the wrong spirit, they can become a burden that crushes the conscientious and puffs up the successful.

Torrey knew this danger better than his manner sometimes suggests. He warned against a life governed by rules, calling it bondage. He insisted that a Christian who stumbles should go straight to his Father, confess, believe he is forgiven because God says so, and go on light-hearted. He said that it is base ingratitude to brood over sins God has cancelled. The same certainty that made his demands so sharp made his comfort so solid. Hold on to both.

Two things to carry

First, take God at His word. When your feelings contradict His promises, believe the promises. When a doubt arises, face it honestly and on your knees. When a command is plain, obey it. When a warning is given, heed it. Most of what Torrey became, he became by doing this.

God is not a man, that he should lie; neither the son of man, that he should repent: hath he said, and shall he not do it? or hath he spoken, and shall he not make it good? NUMBERS 23:19

Second, ask. Ask for the Holy Spirit, for power in whatever service God has given you, and for the salvation of people you know by name. Ask definitely, ask in faith, ask according to His will, and keep asking. Torrey’s whole life was built on the conviction that God gives to those who ask, and most of us have not because we ask not.

A last word about the man

We have been honest about his limits. His teaching on the baptism with the Holy Spirit as a distinct experience after conversion is disputed by many careful readers, and it should be held with an open hand, with Ephesians 5:18 at least as prominent as Acts 2. His seven steps can harden into a technique. His certainty could become bluntness and his bluntness harshness; he spoke of opponents in ways a gentle reader will regret, and he stated alternatives more starkly than truth always allows. His apologetics bear the marks of an age that expected evidence to settle every question. And on hell he used imagery and rhetoric that go beyond what Scripture requires, even where his substance was the historic faith.

None of this has been said to diminish him. It has been said because his own method requires it. He taught his students to test everything by the Word of God, and he would not want to be exempt.

Not unto us, O LORD, not unto us, but unto thy name give glory, for thy mercy, and for thy truth’s sake. PSALM 115:1

He died at Asheville in October 1928, in his seventy-third year. He had been a sceptic who was answered, a pastor who lived by prayer, a teacher who trained a generation, and an evangelist who stood before some of the largest audiences of his time. But those who knew him best remembered something quieter: a man of regular, uninterrupted prayer and daily Bible study, who kept the habits of a small room while he stood before great crowds. The young man who had resolved one night at Yale to end his life, and who instead found himself on his knees, promised God that he would go wherever he was sent. He kept the promise. The God who had kept His word to him kept it to the end.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Return to the chapter of this book that made you least comfortable. Choose one application point and practise it for a month.

2. Ask whether any of Torrey’s counsel has become a new law to you. If so, bring it to God and receive it again as grace.

3. Write down three promises of God you will deliberately believe this week, whatever your feelings.

4. Begin, or renew, a daily list of people to pray for by name, and ask God for the Spirit’s power to speak to them.

5. Choose one of Torrey’s own books from the Reader’s Guide that follows, and begin it this week.

A PRAYER
Faithful God, You have spoken plainly, and You mean what You say. Forgive me for the promises I have not believed and the commands I have not obeyed.
Teach me to take You at Your word as Your servant Reuben Torrey did, and keep me from turning Your counsel into a new law.
Fill me with Your Holy Spirit, teach me to pray, and give me a love for those who do not know Christ.
And as You kept Your word to him to the end, keep Your word to me, until I see You face to face. Amen.

fields.title: A Reader’s Guide to R. A. Torrey
fields.body_html:
Thy words were found, and I did eat them; and thy word was unto me the joy and rejoicing of mine heart: for I am called by thy name, O LORD God of hosts. JEREMIAH 15:16

Torrey is one of the easiest classic writers to read. He wrote plainly, arranged his material under numbered heads, and nearly always told the reader what to do next. He also wrote a great deal — more than forty books — and repeated himself freely, so that the same teaching and even the same stories turn up in several places. The guide below is meant to save the reader time.

Begin here

How to Pray. His best-known book: short, practical chapters on the importance of prayer, praying to God, praying in the name of Christ and according to His will, praying in the Spirit, persevering, and hindrances to prayer. Not yet in the Ochorus library, but widely available.

How to Succeed in the Christian Life. A handbook for new Christians on beginning right, confessing Christ, assurance, Bible study, prayer, work, companions and guidance. The best single introduction to Torrey’s practical teaching. In the Ochorus library.

The Person and Work of the Holy Spirit. His fullest treatment of the Spirit, from His personality to His work in the believer, in prayer and in the prophets. The chapters on the Spirit as a Person, as Teacher and in prayer are among his best. In the Ochorus library.

On the Holy Spirit

Baptism with the Holy Spirit. A short book setting out his distinctive teaching: what the baptism is, why it is needed, the seven steps to receive it, refillings, and how power is lost. The last two chapters are the most valuable. In the Ochorus library, and best read with chapters four to six of this volume.

On the Bible and the faith

The Fundamental Doctrines of the Christian Faith. Sermons preached to his Los Angeles congregation on inspiration, the doctrine of God, the deity and humanity of Christ, the Spirit, the atonement, justification, the new birth, the resurrection, the devil and future punishment. Dense with texts and sharp in tone, but the clearest statement of what he believed. In the Ochorus library.

How to Study the Bible for Greatest Profit and What the Bible Teaches. The first gives methods; the second gathers what Scripture says on each great subject, arranged as propositions with proof texts. Useful reference books. Not yet in the Ochorus library.

Difficulties in the Bible. His answers to alleged errors and contradictions. Some of the answers have dated; the spirit of honest engagement has not. Not yet in the Ochorus library.

On prayer and evangelism

How to Bring Men to Christ. His handbook for personal work, with Scripture for every kind of person and a closing chapter of hints that every Christian can use. In the Ochorus library.

The Power of Prayer and the Prayer of Power. A later book on prayer, gathering many of his convictions and experiences. Not yet in the Ochorus library.

Sermons. Fourteen of his evangelistic sermons are in the Ochorus library, including The Greatest Sentence That Was Ever Written, The Great Attraction: The Uplifted Christ, The Most Important Question, Excuses, Refuges of Lies and The Day of Golden Opportunity. They show the evangelist at work. Read them aloud if you can; they were made to be heard.

Approach with care

Baptism with the Holy Spirit and the chapter on it in The Person and Work of the Holy Spirit present a disputed view, and they are best read with 1 Corinthians 12:13 and Ephesians 5:18 open beside them. The two sermons on hell at the end of The Fundamental Doctrines are serious and honest but lurid in places. And Torrey’s polemic against Christian Science, Unitarians and liberal ministers, scattered through his doctrinal sermons, reflects the controversies of his day; take the substance, not the scorn.

About Torrey

Roger Martin, R. A. Torrey: Apostle of Certainty (1976), is the standard modern life, sympathetic and well documented. George T. B. Davis, Torrey and Alexander: The Story of a World-Wide Revival (1905), is a contemporary account of the great missions, written in the glow of the events. The Ochorus author page carries a shorter biography.

Three counsels for reading him

Read him with the Bible open. His method was to pile up texts and dare the reader to check them. Check them.

Read him for the practice rather than the scheme. Where he gives numbered steps or conditions, take them as a searching of the heart, not as a formula that obliges God.

And read him on your knees. He believed that truth which did not lead to prayer and action had not yet done its work. Stop at the end of a chapter and do the next thing he tells you, or pray instead of reading on.

Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth. 2 TIMOTHY 2:15
